The indictment was returned on October 30 and unsealed this month; he has pleaded not guilty, and his lawyers say he was unjustly profiled and unlawfully arrested.
articles.body: Rod Wave, the 28-year-old rapper whose legal name is Rodarius Green, has been indicted in Fulton County, Georgia, on drug and weapons charges arising from an Atlanta traffic stop last November. According to the indictment obtained by Rolling Stone, Green was driving at least 15 miles over the posted speed limit and disregarded a traffic control device in a highly residential area of Atlanta along Defoor Avenue when he was pulled over for reckless driving on November 7, 2025. The indictment alleges he unlawfully possessed oxycodone and had a gun within arm's reach; police say they found a black .40 caliber Glock with a high-capacity magazine in his waistband, along with suspected oxycodone and promethazine in the vehicle. The charges include possession of a Schedule II controlled substance, possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, and reckless driving. Green was booked on the charges and released the following day on an $8,000 bond. His attorneys, Drew Findling, Marissa Goldberg and Zack Findling, strongly dispute the allegations, telling TMZ their client was unjustly profiled and unlawfully arrested. The arrest came on the same day Green earned his first-ever Grammy nomination, for Best Song Written for Visual Media, for his track "Sinners" from the 2025 film of the same name. The indictment, returned October 30 and unsealed this month, is an accusation, not a finding of guilt, and the case will now proceed through the courts. Rod Wave also faces a separate Georgia case involving an April 2025 incident at his home.

articles.title: Cody Johnson to skip CMA Awards due to "mental and physical exhaustion"
articles.description: Country star Cody Johnson will skip the CMA Awards, citing mental and physical exhaustion. The announcement, reported by Rolling Stone on November 17, comes as Johnson has been one of country music's hardest-touring and most in-demand acts. His withdrawal puts a spotlight on burnout in a genre that prizes relentless road work.
articles.body: Cody Johnson, one of country music's biggest current stars, will not attend the CMA Awards, telling fans he is stepping back due to mental and physical exhaustion. The news was reported by Rolling Stone on November 17, just ahead of country music's biggest night. Johnson has built his career on a punishing touring schedule and a reputation for outworking his peers, moving from Texas dancehalls to stadiums and major award nominations without slowing down. His decision to publicly cite exhaustion, rather than a scheduling conflict or vague personal reasons, is notable in a genre where toughness and constant touring are part of the brand. It echoes a wider conversation in the music industry about burnout, as artists from across genres have cancelled or scaled back tours in recent years to protect their health. For the CMA Awards, Johnson's absence removes one of the night's prominent names from the room. For fans, the frankness of the reason may matter as much as the absence itself, signalling that even country's hardest-working stars are setting limits.

articles.title: Travis Scott and Don Toliver sued for copyright infringement over 2019 hit "What to Do?"
articles.description: Travis Scott and Don Toliver are being sued for copyright infringement over their 2019 hit "What to Do?", Rolling Stone reports. The lawsuit adds another high-profile copyright case to a hip-hop landscape already crowded with disputes over sampling and songwriting credit. Details of the claim and the plaintiffs were not fully set out in the initial reporting.
articles.body: Travis Scott and Don Toliver have been sued for copyright infringement over "What to Do?", their 2019 collaboration, according to Rolling Stone. The track dates from the period when Toliver was breaking through as a Cactus Jack artist under Scott's wing, and it remains one of the best-known songs from their early partnership. Copyright suits over songs of that era have become common as older hits are re-examined, with plaintiffs ranging from fellow songwriters to owners of sampled material. The case lands as Toliver is in the news for a different reason, announcing his sixth album "Nitrous" this week, so the lawsuit and the album news arrive together. For Scott, it is another legal entanglement alongside the long-running litigation around the Astroworld tragedy, though this is a purely commercial copyright dispute. The filing underscores how the value of streaming-era catalogs keeps old songs in legal play years after release, since a hit from 2019 can still generate significant royalties. The outcome will turn on the specifics of the claim, which were not fully detailed in the initial report.

articles.title: Don Toliver announces sixth album "Nitrous" with slick trailer
articles.description: Don Toliver has announced his sixth album, "Nitrous", unveiling it with a slick trailer, Rolling Stone reports. The announcement sets up his next full-length release as he continues a run of high-profile collaborations and festival headline slots. A release date and tracklist were not included in the initial announcement coverage.
articles.body: Don Toliver has announced his sixth studio album, "Nitrous", revealing the project with a polished trailer that Rolling Stone covered this week. The announcement is the first concrete news of a new full-length from the Houston rapper since his recent run of albums and guest appearances kept him near the top of the hip-hop charts. Toliver has built his career on melodic, atmospheric rap and a string of high-profile collaborations, including his work with Travis Scott's Cactus Jack label, and "Nitrous" arrives with that momentum behind it. The trailer-led reveal follows the modern rollout playbook, building anticipation with visuals before any music is released. Fans will now be watching for a release date, tracklist and any guest features, which Toliver typically keeps under wraps until close to launch. The announcement comes in the same week that Toliver and Scott were named in a copyright lawsuit over their 2019 hit "What to Do?", giving the album news a complicated backdrop. Even so, "Nitrous" is positioned as one of the more anticipated rap releases of the coming months.

articles.title: Noah Kahan addresses Grammy snub in the most Noah Kahan way: "Let's move on together"
articles.description: Noah Kahan has addressed his absence from the 2027 Grammy nominations with characteristic self-deprecation, telling fans "let's move on together." The folk-pop star's response, reported by Rolling Stone, stands out for its grace in a week when several artists and their fans have loudly protested snubs. Kahan, whose earnest songwriting made him one of the biggest breakout acts of recent years, chose to defuse the moment rather than fuel it.
articles.body: Noah Kahan has responded to being left out of the 2027 Grammy nominations in the most Noah Kahan way possible, with a self-deprecating message urging fans to move on together. The folk-pop singer-songwriter, who became one of the biggest breakout stars of recent years on the strength of his confessional songwriting and the album "Stick Season", was among the notable names absent when the Recording Academy announced the nominees on November 16. Where other snubs this year have sparked angry reactions from artists and fan campaigns, Kahan chose to defuse the moment, acknowledging the disappointment without turning it into a grievance. His tone fits the persona that made him popular in the first place: earnest, funny and allergic to self-importance. The 2027 nominations were led by RAYE with 11 and ROSALÍA with 9, and the field also produced talking points around Harry Styles being blanked and BTS receiving no nominations. Kahan's response may be the most graceful of the week, and it is likely to endear him further to a fanbase that values his candour. The Grammys take place on February 7, 2027, in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Blink-182 and Pierce the Veil lead When We Were Young 2027 festival lineup
articles.description: Blink-182 and Pierce the Veil will headline the When We Were Young festival in 2027, Rolling Stone reports. The Las Vegas festival, built on emo and pop-punk nostalgia, continues to draw the genre's biggest names for its next edition. The full lineup announcement sets up another large-scale gathering for a scene that has stayed commercially strong.
articles.body: Blink-182 and Pierce the Veil will lead the lineup for the 2027 edition of the When We Were Young festival, Rolling Stone reports. The Las Vegas festival has become the flagship event for emo, pop-punk and adjacent scenes, selling out on the strength of nostalgia lineups that reunite the bands who defined the genre in the 2000s. Blink-182's headline slot continues the band's remarkable second act, having returned to stadiums and festivals after reuniting with Tom DeLonge, while Pierce the Veil's prominent billing reflects their enduring draw with the festival's core audience. When We Were Young has grown from a one-off nostalgia event into a recurring fixture on the festival calendar, with each year's lineup announcement treated as a major moment for the scene. The 2027 bill will be watched for how it balances legacy headliners against newer acts, since the festival's long-term health depends on refreshing its audience as well as serving the original fans. Ticket details and the full undercard were not included in the initial report.

articles.title: Julien Baker reveals "This World or the Next," their first new album in six years
articles.description: Julien Baker has announced "This World or the Next," their first new album in six years, Rolling Stone reports. The announcement marks a return to solo work for the acclaimed singer-songwriter, who has spent recent years in collaborative projects including boygenius. Fans have been waiting years for a follow-up, and the announcement is one of the week's most anticipated album reveals.
articles.body: Julien Baker has revealed "This World or the Next," their first new album in six years, according to Rolling Stone. The announcement ends a long wait for a follow-up from one of indie music's most respected songwriters, whose stark, confessional songs have earned a devoted following. Baker's recent years have been dominated by collaboration, most notably boygenius, the supergroup with Phoebe Bridgers and Lucy Dacus that won multiple Grammys and became one of the defining indie acts of the decade. A return to solo work is therefore a significant moment, promising the intimate, guitar-led songwriting that made Baker's name before the group took off. The six-year gap underscores how fully the collaborative era consumed her schedule, and how much anticipation has built for new solo material. Details of the album's release date, tracklist and lead single were announced alongside the reveal. For indie fans, "This World or the Next" is likely to be one of the most closely watched releases of the coming months.

articles.title: Jonny Greenwood and Dudu Tassa return with new album and lead single
articles.description: Jonny Greenwood and Dudu Tassa are back with a new album and a lead single, Rolling Stone reports. The Radiohead guitarist and the Israeli musician have continued one of the most distinctive cross-cultural collaborations in modern music, blending Middle Eastern sounds with Greenwood's experimental sensibilities. The new record follows their earlier work together, which drew critical acclaim.
articles.body: Jonny Greenwood, the Radiohead guitarist, and Israeli musician Dudu Tassa have announced a new album together, releasing a lead single alongside the news, according to Rolling Stone. The pair's collaboration is one of the most unusual and acclaimed partnerships in contemporary music, combining Tassa's Middle Eastern musical heritage with Greenwood's experimental guitar work and compositional ambition. Their previous album together, "Jarak Qaribak", released in 2023, was praised for its seamless fusion of Arabic song forms with art-rock textures, and it toured internationally. A new record suggests the partnership has deepened from a one-off project into an ongoing creative relationship. Greenwood remains one of the most restlessly creative figures in rock, balancing Radiohead, film scoring and side projects, and his work with Tassa is among the most personal of them. The lead single offers the first taste of where the new album is headed, and further details on the release date and tracklist are expected to follow. For fans of either artist, the announcement is a welcome return from a collaboration that has consistently produced something neither could make alone.

articles.title: Bobby Helms' "Jingle Bell Rock" re-enters Hot 100 at No. 28, nearly 70 years after release
articles.description: Bobby Helms' "Jingle Bell Rock" has re-entered the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 28 on the chart dated November 21, 2026, in its 69th total week on the chart. The song was first released in October 1957, 69 years ago, and last appeared on the Hot 100 in January 2026. It leads a wave of Christmas songs, with Brenda Lee's "Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree" at No. 30, Wham!'s "Last Christmas" climbing to No. 14 and Mariah Carey at No. 18.
articles.body: Christmas has arrived early on the Billboard Hot 100, with Bobby Helms' "Jingle Bell Rock" re-entering the chart at No. 28 on the survey dated November 21, 2026. The song was first released in October 1957, which makes this its 69th total week on the Hot 100, a longevity record that few songs in history can match. It last appeared on the chart dated January 3, 2026, during the previous holiday season, and its return this week puts it ahead of most current hits. Helms himself once questioned whether rock 'n' roll belonged at Christmas, yet the song peaked at No. 2 on the Hot 100 last Christmas, higher than most new songs ever reach. It is not alone: Brenda Lee's "Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree" returns two places below it at No. 30, Wham!'s "Last Christmas" climbs from No. 37 to No. 14, and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" reaches No. 18 before Thanksgiving. The Hot 100 combines streaming, radio audience and sales, so the holiday surge reflects genuine listening rather than a chart quirk. Eight Christmas songs now sit on the Hot 100, and Wham! remains the top-ranking holiday hit so far. The early arrival of the Christmas wave, weeks before December, shows how the holiday streaming season now starts in mid-November.

articles.title: Lil Baby lands 8 new Hot 100 entries as "Fresh" debuts at No. 2 on the Billboard 200
articles.description: Lil Baby has added eight new entries to the Billboard Hot 100 from his new album "Fresh", bringing his career total to 168 hits — the seventh-highest tally in the chart's 68-year history. The album itself debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 with 59,000 equivalent album units, just 3,000 behind Olivia Rodrigo's chart-topping album. Nine of the album's 17 tracks are now on the Hot 100.
articles.body: Lil Baby has made chart history this week, landing eight new entries on the Billboard Hot 100 from his November 6-released album "Fresh". The new entries lift his career total to 168 Hot 100 hits, the seventh-highest tally of all time, behind only Drake (408), Taylor Swift (281), Future (248), the "Glee" cast (207), Lil Wayne (195) and Kanye West (177). Before Monday, November 16, only five acts in the chart's 68-year history had passed 160 hits, and Lil Baby is now the sixth to join that group. Of the 14 songs that appeared on the Hot 100 for the first time this week, eight belong to "Fresh", with "Mr. Do Something" at No. 48, "Top Uh It" at No. 60 and "All My Partnas" featuring Future, Young Thug and Rylo Rodriguez at No. 69. Alongside the previously charted "Dead Fresh" at No. 25, nine of the album's 17 tracks are now on the Hot 100, more than half the project. The chart news follows the album's debut at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 with first-week sales of 59,000 equivalent album units, roughly 3,000 behind Olivia Rodrigo's fifth week at No. 1 with 62,000 units. Morgan Wallen held No. 3 with about 50,000 units, while P1Harmony's "BLOW UP" entered at No. 4. The narrow gap at the top makes this one of the closest Billboard 200 races of the year.

articles.title: DistroKid hands AI upload data to UMG and Sony for Suno lawsuit after initial refusal
articles.description: DistroKid has complied with a subpoena from Universal Music Group and Sony Music, handing over data on how much AI-generated music flows through its platform, according to a Monday, November 16 court filing obtained by Billboard. The distributor initially refused to provide the data, prompting the labels to go to court last month to force compliance. The labels say the data is key to proving Suno-generated music is eating into their market share and royalty distributions.
articles.body: DistroKid has provided Universal Music Group and Sony Music with data about the prevalence of AI-generated music moving through its platform, according to a court filing on Monday, November 16 obtained by Billboard. The filing says DistroKid has complied with a third-party subpoena served by the labels as part of their copyright infringement lawsuit against AI music service Suno, and the subpoena petition has now been withdrawn. The subpoena sought numbers on how much of the music passing through the leading DIY digital distributor is thought to be made with Suno and other AI generators. DistroKid initially refused to hand over the data, leading the labels to initiate legal action last month to force compliance, but the distributor has since produced responsive documents. UMG and Sony say the data is key to proving that Suno-generated music is eating into their market share and royalty distributions, a central plank of their damages case. DistroKid is not a party to the Suno suit, but the labels' separate lawsuit against the distributor remains live: filed in September, it alleges DistroKid flooded streamers with "mass AI-generated, SEO-optimized, and copyright-infringing slop" and engaged in deceptive business practices. Representatives for DistroKid and Sony declined to comment on Tuesday, November 17, and UMG did not return a request for comment. The data handover gives the labels a powerful new evidentiary source as the Suno case moves forward.

articles.title: SoundCloud CEO: "Wishing away the advent of AI music is not a strategy"
articles.description: SoundCloud CEO Eliah Seton has set out the platform's AI policies in a Billboard interview published November 17, arguing that "wishing away the advent of AI music is not a strategy." The interview coincides with SoundCloud's crackdown on "AI slop, spam, and excessive uploads," announced the same week, with release-volume limits, account terminations and other penalties on the table. SoundCloud, which has partnered with ElevenMusic and Moises in the past month, is positioning itself as an artist-first platform in the AI era.
articles.body: SoundCloud CEO Eliah Seton has laid out the company's approach to AI in a Billboard interview published November 17, with the blunt message that "wishing away the advent of AI music is not a strategy." The interview came as SoundCloud formally kicked off a crackdown on "AI slop, spam, and excessive uploads," disclosed by Seton in a blog post titled "AI Is Changing Music. Its Future Must Be Built Around Artists." In the post, Seton wrote that "AI slop has no place on SoundCloud" and that the company is "drawing a clear line against AI slop, spam, and excessive uploads that overwhelm the platform, interfere with music discovery, or undermine the experience for artists and fans." Updated community guidelines now describe excessive uploading as something that brings no value to the user experience, and users who submit an excessive amount of uploads may face upload limits, additional review, account termination or other penalties. The terms also bar using AI to deceive, including to game systems, manipulate monetization or earnings, or mislead users about authenticity, with payouts subject to withholding or reversal. Seton warned that AI "presents existential risks if managed wrong," but argued the answer is artist-centered rules, not denial. SoundCloud has partnered with ElevenMusic and Moises during the past month, signalling it wants to work with legitimate AI tools while policing abuse. The crackdown puts SoundCloud among the most active platforms in drawing a line between useful AI and spam.

articles.title: ILLIT climbs Billboard charts for a third straight week as "You're Under Arrest" hits new peaks
articles.description: ILLIT continues its Billboard chart climb as "You're Under Arrest" reaches new peaks for a third consecutive week. The single now sits at No. 12 on Global Excl. U.S., No. 22 on the Billboard Global 200 and No. 8 on Hot Dance/Pop Songs, while mini-album "BREAK EVEN" holds No. 2 on World Albums and Top Album Sales and No. 44 on the Billboard 200. This is a genuine new development on the ILLIT chart story covered Nov 16–17 (multiple weeks on the Billboard 200), with the Global 200 climb the new element.
articles.body: ILLIT's rise on the Billboard charts has continued for a third consecutive week, with new single "You're Under Arrest" reaching fresh peaks on the rankings released November 17 and dated November 21. The track now sits at No. 12 on Global Excl. U.S., No. 22 on the Billboard Global 200 and No. 8 on Hot Dance/Pop Songs, extending an unusually steady upward trajectory. On the Global 200, which tracks streaming across more than 200 countries and territories, the song debuted at No. 150 on the November 7 chart, jumped to No. 24 the following week and climbed another two places to No. 22 on the latest survey. The group's fifth mini-album, "BREAK EVEN", is performing strongly as well, claiming No. 2 on both the World Albums and Top Album Sales charts and landing at No. 44 on the Billboard 200. ILLIT also reached No. 58 on the Artist 100, the highest position among K-pop girl groups entering the chart this week. As of November 17, the group had approximately 20.45 million monthly listeners on Spotify. ILLIT will next appear at the 2026 MAMA Awards, taking place November 20–21 at Kyocera Dome Osaka in Japan, where a high-profile performance could push the single higher still.

articles.title: The Geo-Located Generation: What Nonstop Surveillance Is Doing to Children
articles.author: Sarah Zhang
articles.description: The Atlantic’s December cover story asks what happens to children — and their parents — when every step can be tracked, and it ends with a plea to let kids do things on their own again.
articles.body:
Sarah Zhang’s cover story for The Atlantic’s December issue starts from a simple observation: parents today can functionally track their children around the clock, from birth through adulthood, and most of them do. The tools start with products like the Snoo smart bassinet and Apple AirTags sewn into toddler backpacks, and they run through school portals, WhatsApp parent groups and location-sharing apps like Find My Friends and Life360. Zhang examines what this constant surveillance is doing to children — above all to their resilience and independence — and what it is doing to their parents, who are becoming more anxious even as they gain more information.

The piece is built around reporting and research rather than polemic. Zhang quotes a UK study that found the share of children aged seven and eight walking to school alone fell from 80 percent in 1971 to 6 percent in 2010, and she tells the story of a mother in a Facebook group for college parents who, seeing her daughter’s phone still in her room ten minutes before a maths test, typed: “Could someone ask their kid to go knock on her door?” Developmental psychology, Zhang writes, suggests that constant monitoring eventually becomes unhealthy for children, partly because they absorb the sense that danger lurks around every corner, and partly because they never get to solve problems on their own. Parents, too, are supposed to undergo their own transformation as children grow, relinquishing knowledge and control — and the apps make that relinquishing almost impossible.

The story’s centre of gravity is the work of psychologist Camilo Ortiz, who with a colleague invented “independence therapy”: for several weeks, anxious children do one new thing on their own every day, and their parents have to let them. One of the first participants was a nine-year-old girl who was afraid to sleep in her own bed; she chose to ride the city bus by herself, missed her stop, found a grown-up who helped her backtrack, and slept in her own bed that night for the first time. Zhang also gives generous space to Lenore Skenazy and the Let Grow movement, which she credits with a decade of arguing for childhood independence, and notes that thirteen US states have now passed reasonable-childhood-independence laws and more than a thousand schools have assigned the Let Grow Experience. The cover story ends with a plea: let kids start doing things on their own, and everyone is better off — the kids, the parents, the community.

articles.title: Venezuela’s Collaborator-in-Chief
articles.author: Jon Lee Anderson
articles.description: Jon Lee Anderson reports on Delcy Rodríguez and the new American imperialism in Venezuela — the most consequential piece in this week’s New Yorker on a story that is still unfolding.
articles.body:
Jon Lee Anderson’s piece in the November 23 issue of The New Yorker examines Venezuela through the figure of Delcy Rodríguez, the country’s leader in the aftermath of the American intervention, and asks what her rule reveals about a new American imperialism. Anderson is one of the magazine’s most experienced foreign correspondents, and the piece draws on his long reporting history in Latin America to place the current moment in a longer story of US involvement in the region.

The article sits alongside Anne Applebaum’s piece in The Atlantic’s December issue, “After the Apocalypse,” which covers how Venezuela struggles to recover and how the US is exploiting the country for oil and money — a sign of how central Venezuela has become to the foreign-policy debate. Anderson’s focus is on Rodríguez herself: how she governs, whom she relies on, and what her collaboration with Washington means for Venezuelans who lived through years of crisis under Maduro. The question at the heart of the piece is whether the new order is a genuine break with the past or a different kind of domination wearing a friendlier face.

For readers following the story, the piece is valuable because it goes beyond the headlines about oil and sanctions to the politics of collaboration itself: who benefits, who is sidelined, and what happens to a country when its future is negotiated between its own leaders and a foreign power. It is the kind of reported essay that The New Yorker does best — patient, sourced, and sceptical of easy narratives from any side.

articles.title: The Buddhist A.I. Sect That Wants to Take Over Silicon Valley
articles.author: Sam Kriss
articles.description: A strange and gripping reported piece on MAPLE, a Buddhist-flavoured AI group whose public mission is teaching us how to live with AI — and whose secret mission, Kriss reports, is much stranger.
articles.body:
Sam Kriss’s piece in the November 23 issue of The New Yorker takes readers inside MAPLE, a group that promises to teach us how to live in the age of AI, and reports that its secret mission is much stranger than its public one. The piece is filed under Annals of Religion, which is a clue to its tone: Kriss treats MAPLE not just as a tech story but as a religious one, examining how a spiritual vocabulary has attached itself to the most powerful technology of the moment.

The context is a striking one. In the past few years, more than a dozen senior AI researchers have quit their posts, saying the kinds of things that you used to hear only from people on the street. Jacob Coxon, formerly of Anthropic, walked out with the warning that “there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future.” Against that background of genuine existential dread among the people building the systems, groups like MAPLE offer something between a philosophy and a refuge: a framework for living with machines that may outthink us, wrapped in Buddhist language about attention, attachment and liberation.

What makes the piece worth reading is that Kriss neither mocks nor endorses. He reports what MAPLE actually teaches and asks, what its members actually believe, and what it means that Silicon Valley’s response to the fear of extinction is increasingly taking the form of a sect. For anyone who has wondered why the AI debate keeps sliding from engineering into theology, this is the piece that explains the slide — and why it might matter more than the engineering.

articles.title: Why We Can’t Look Away from Medea
articles.author: Anahid Nersessian
articles.description: A sharp essay on Edith Hall’s new history of Medea — and on why, when a mother kills her children, we reach for diagnosis instead of tragedy.
articles.body:
Anahid Nersessian’s essay in the November 23 issue of The New Yorker takes Edith Hall’s new history of Medea as its starting point and asks a question that is really about us: when a mother kills her children, why do we reach for diagnosis, and what do we lose by doing so? Hall’s book gives Medea, the original murderous mother, what Nersessian calls the “girlboss treatment” — a reframing that makes the ancient figure newly legible to a contemporary audience. Nersessian’s interest is in what that reframing reveals and what it obscures.

The essay’s argument is that our therapeutic categories — trauma, pathology, disorder — obscure what the Greeks knew about tragedy and what we forget at our peril. Medea’s story is not a case study; it is a tragedy, and tragedy works by a different logic than diagnosis. It asks us to sit with actions that cannot be explained away, and with a figure whose motives remain partly opaque even to herself. To reduce her to a syndrome is to make her manageable, and to miss the point.

Nersessian writes as a critic who knows the classical material deeply and is impatient with both easy moralising and easy psychologising. The essay is a pleasure to read for its sentences alone, but its real value is the way it uses an ancient story to diagnose a modern habit: our preference for explanations that let us look away from the thing itself. It is the most literary piece in this week’s selection, and the one most likely to change how you think about a story you thought you knew.

articles.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business
articles.author: Isabella Ward
articles.description: WIRED’s feature on how two Google and Apple alumni used AI to design munitions — a frontline report on Silicon Valley’s turn toward the arms business.
articles.body:
Isabella Ward’s WIRED feature, published on November 17, follows Chad Steelberg and Andy Baynes — Google and Apple alumni — as they apply what they learned running software companies and designing iPhones to manufacturing lethal munitions. The pair built an AI model to help decide how to get involved in Ukraine’s war, and the system moved from internal research to a product called GRAIL, which Steelberg says automates supply-chain management and compliance and simulates weapons against targets across different environments and weather conditions.

The business behind the story is Tiberius Aerospace, Steelberg’s defence venture, which has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships and a defence-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management led its financing round. The company announced its first successful Sceptre projectile firing from a NATO-standard 155-millimetre howitzer in April, is working with the US Army to mature the system, and has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license and distribute the munition. Its missile, still in development, is expected to start generating revenue next year.

What makes the piece important is not just the company but the pattern it represents. The AI industry’s turn toward defence is no longer a fringe story: Google has signed classified Pentagon deals, OpenAI has revised its policies, and a generation of founders who once built consumer software is now building weapons with the same tools and the same pitch — move fast, use AI, disrupt an old industry. Ward’s reporting is careful about what the AI actually did and what it did not, crediting the AI-assisted prototype without assuming battlefield effectiveness. The question it leaves is the one the whole sector is avoiding: what happens when the people who decide how wars are fought are the people who used to decide how phones are designed?

articles.title: I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa
articles.author: Abdelrahman ElGendy
articles.description: A National Book Award finalist writes about being denied a US visa days before the ceremony — a first-person account of what the new immigration politics feels like from the inside.
articles.body:
Abdelrahman ElGendy, an Egyptian writer and translator whose memoir Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming is a finalist for the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction, writes in The New Yorker about being denied a US visa days before the ceremony. ElGendy had hoped to travel to New York for the November 18 awards ceremony, where the winners are announced. Instead, after his application was placed in administrative processing, he learned that his visa had been denied, with no specific explanation given.

The essay’s power comes from the story behind it. ElGendy was seventeen when he was arrested at a demonstration in Cairo in 2013, two years after the January 25 revolution, and he spent six years as a political prisoner, writing his memoir steadily and smuggling the pages out one visit at a time. He fled Egypt, moved constantly between countries in search of a visa and a semblance of home, and in 2022 received a full ride to pursue an MFA in nonfiction at the University of Pittsburgh. He left the United States in 2025 amid concerns about immigration enforcement and the possibility of being returned to Egypt, where he feared further persecution.

At the visa interview, the consular officer nodded at the Penguin Random House letterhead and the printout of the National Book Foundation page, seemed reassured that his flights and accommodation were fully covered, and squinted and nodded at his European residence permit. Then came the line: “Unfortunately, I can’t decide on this application now. We have to consult Washington first, then get back to you.” The next morning he woke to a formal denial in his inbox. They would not put in writing what the system had flagged or the reason Washington provided overnight, only that he was found ineligible for a visitor visa under the Immigration and Nationality Act. It is a short essay, but it says more about the state of American openness than a shelf of policy papers — a writer who survived an Egyptian prison cannot get into the country to accept a literary prize.

articles.title: Russia moves to raise the military service age limit for women amid troop shortages
articles.description: Russia's State Duma has passed in first reading a bill that would raise the maximum age for women to serve in the military, Meduza reports. The move comes as Russia faces mounting troop shortages nearly four years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the war now in its 1,728th day. It is the latest sign that Moscow is widening the pool of people it can draw into the armed forces.
articles.body: Russia's State Duma has passed in its first reading a bill that would raise the maximum age for women to serve in the military, Meduza reports. The change would widen the pool of women eligible for military service at a time when Russia is facing mounting troop shortages, with the full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its 1,728th day and Russian personnel losses estimated by Kyiv at more than 1.6 million. The bill is the latest in a series of measures Moscow has taken to sustain its war effort without declaring a full mobilisation — which the Kremlin has avoided since the deeply unpopular partial mobilisation of autumn 2022. Other recent steps reported by Meduza include proposals to shield war participants' property from bankruptcy seizure, a sweetener aimed at keeping the war's veterans and their families on side. Raising the service age for women is a quieter, bureaucratic lever, but it points in the same direction: the Russian military needs more people, and the Kremlin is reaching further into the population to find them.

articles.title: Russia strikes Dnipro in the evening, wounding three and damaging Austria's consulate
articles.description: Russian forces attacked the city of Dnipro on Tuesday evening, wounding three people and damaging the building of Austria's consulate, Ukrainska Pravda reports as its lead story. The strike was the latest in a day of attacks on Ukrainian cities that also saw Vinnytsia hit twice. Dnipro, a major city in central-eastern Ukraine, has been a regular target of Russian missile and drone attacks.
articles.body: Russian forces attacked Dnipro on Tuesday evening, wounding three people and damaging the building of Austria's consulate in the city, Ukrainska Pravda reported as its lead story. Photos from the scene showed damage to the consular building, making it the latest case of a foreign diplomatic mission being caught in a Russian strike on a Ukrainian city. The Dnipro attack came on a day of heavy Russian strikes across Ukraine: Vinnytsia was hit twice, with a fire breaking out in the city centre and four people injured, and Russian drones also pushed into Moldovan airspace, forcing Chisinau to close its skies. The attacks continue a pattern of Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure and cities far from the front line, and they land the same week the UN reported a sharp rise in civilian deaths in Ukraine. Diplomatic damage of this kind tends to draw formal protests from the affected country, and Austria is likely to raise the consulate strike with Moscow.

articles.title: UN: Russia killed at least 372 Ukrainian civilians in October — 95% more than a year ago
articles.description: Russia killed at least 372 civilians in Ukraine in October, the United Nations said — 95% more than in the same month last year. The figure, reported by Ukrainska Pravda, underlines how sharply the civilian toll has risen as Russia intensifies strikes on cities and energy infrastructure ahead of winter. The UN's count is a verified minimum, meaning the true toll is likely higher.
articles.body: Russia killed at least 372 civilians in Ukraine during October, the United Nations said, a figure 95% higher than in October last year, Ukrainska Pravda reported on Tuesday. The UN's monitoring mission counts only deaths it has been able to verify, so the real toll is almost certainly higher — and it does not include casualties in occupied territory, where verification is often impossible. The jump reflects Russia's intensifying campaign against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure as winter approaches, including the mass drone and missile attacks that have knocked out power in nine regions and forced emergency outage schedules. October's toll comes alongside other grim markers reported this week: the death toll from the November 15 strike on a humanitarian aid point in Komyshuvakha rose to 72, and Tuesday brought fresh attacks on Dnipro and Vinnytsia. The UN figures are the closest thing to an authoritative count of the war's civilian cost, and Kyiv is expected to cite them in pressing partners for more air-defence systems.

articles.title: Russian drones force Moldova to close its airspace and six border crossings
articles.description: Moldova closed its airspace and six border crossings with Ukraine after Russian drones entered its airspace on Tuesday, with one Shahed drone filmed flying over the capital, Chisinau. Seven drones were detected, some of which crashed, and drone debris was later found 50 metres from the Ukrainian border. It is one of the most serious Russian drone incursions into Moldovan airspace of the war.
articles.body: Moldova closed its airspace and six border crossings with Ukraine on Tuesday after Russian drones entered its airspace, Ukrainska Pravda reports. Seven drones were detected over Moldovan territory, some of which crashed, and one Shahed attack drone was filmed flying over the capital, Chisinau, prompting the authorities to shut the country's airspace. Drone debris was later found just 50 metres from the Ukrainian border. The incursion is one of the most serious of the war for Moldova, a small country between Ukraine and Romania that has repeatedly seen Russian missiles and drones cross its skies but has tried to avoid direct confrontation with Moscow. The episode also underlines how Russia's nightly drone barrages against Ukraine keep spilling into neighbouring states — a risk European governments have been warning about as the war drags on. Moldova's pro-European government has aligned itself firmly with Kyiv, and the incident is likely to sharpen its calls for more air-defence support from its partners.

articles.title: The Game Awards 2026 nominees revealed — GTA VI leads with 8, two days before launch
articles.description: Geoff Keighley revealed the nominees for The Game Awards 2026 on Tuesday, and Grand Theft Auto VI leads the field with eight nominations — including Game of the Year — two days before the game even launches on November 19. GTA VI faces 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the top prize. The ceremony is December 10 in Los Angeles, and the nominee reveal was so popular the show's website briefly crashed.
articles.body: Geoff Keighley revealed the nominees for The Game Awards 2026 in a livestream on Tuesday, November 17, and Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI leads all games with eight nominations — including Game of the Year — even though it does not launch until Thursday, November 19. GTA VI is eligible only because the show's cutoff is Friday, November 20 at 9 p.m. PT, one day after release. Its eight nominations cover Game of the Year, Best Game Direction, Best Narrative, Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, Best Audio Design and Best Action/Adventure, plus a Best Performance nod for Manni L. Perez. The Game of the Year field is rounded out by 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, while Nintendo is the most-nominated publisher overall with 12. Fan voting is open now at thegameawards.com and closes December 9, and the winners will be announced at the ceremony on Thursday, December 10 at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, streaming live on Disney+ for the first time alongside YouTube and Twitch. Interest was so high that the show's official site buckled under the traffic during the reveal — a sign of just how much of the industry's year now revolves around a game almost nobody has played yet.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond, Amazon announces
articles.description: Amazon has officially announced that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond, releasing a first teaser for the new 007 film. Pattinson was not on any published shortlist — the reported frontrunners were Jack Lowden, Jacob Elordi and others — and the choice is a surprise. Denis Villeneuve is directing, and Amazon reportedly plans five Bond films plus streaming spin-offs.
articles.body: Amazon has officially announced that British actor Robert Pattinson will become the next James Bond, releasing a first teaser for the new 007 film, GameMAG reports. The casting is a genuine surprise: Pattinson did not appear on any official list of candidates, and the reported frontrunners in August were Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Jack O'Connell and Jack Barton, with Jacob Elordi later emerging as a leader. The picture changed in early November, when Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were reported to have screen-tested — with director Denis Villeneuve said to have invited Pattinson to try out. The choice comes amid upheaval in the superhero world both actors inhabit: DC Studios chiefs James Gunn and Peter Safran were fired, Pattinson's The Batman: Part 2 has stalled for years, and Skydance is reportedly preparing for the failure of Hoult's Superman sequel. Amazon is moving fast: it plans five Bond films plus a series of spin-offs for its streaming service, in part because Ian Fleming's Bond books enter the public domain on January 1, 2035. Pattinson follows Daniel Craig, whose five-film run ended with No Time to Die in 2021.

articles.title: Trump administration dismisses crisis fears after a week of disruptive tech outages
articles.description: Top Trump administration officials moved to reassure Americans after a string of major tech and infrastructure failures disrupted travel, business and banking — a Microsoft outage, an FAA systems failure that grounded thousands of flights, bank outages at Chase and others, and a reported outage on the NSA's classified network. Vice President JD Vance said 'we do not see some crisis coming down', while officials insisted there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack.
articles.body: Top officials from the Trump administration sought to reassure Americans and dismiss fears of a possible crisis after a string of major tech and infrastructure failures disrupted travel, business and banking for millions of people. 'We do not see some crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything,' Vice President JD Vance told Fox News in an interview released Monday, adding that friends had asked him whether they should be building bunkers or stocking up on food and water. The chaotic week began last Thursday with a massive Microsoft outage that knocked out Outlook and Teams worldwide, followed on Friday by an FAA systems failure — blamed on a single newly installed router in Arkansas — that cancelled thousands of flights. On Monday, major banks including Chase reported problems, with Chase blaming a software bug, and United Airlines suffered a short-lived outage. On Tuesday, CNN reported that the highly classified network the NSA uses for internal communications was down, according to six people familiar with the matter. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence the incidents were directly related, and a DHS official said with '98% certainty' this was not a cyberattack. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has meanwhile demanded as much as $50 billion in emergency funding after the FAA ground stop.

articles.title: Universal and Sony fight Suno's bid to freeze second lawsuit, warning its latest AI models could escape scrutiny until 2028
articles.description: Universal Music and Sony Music are fighting Suno's request to freeze their second copyright lawsuit against the AI music company, warning that its newest AI models could escape scrutiny until at least 2028. The labels have offered to defer proving ownership of more than 60,000 recordings, but want discovery into how Suno's v6 model was trained to start now. It is the latest front in the music industry's legal war over AI training data.
articles.body: Universal Music Group and Sony Music are fighting Suno's bid to freeze their second copyright lawsuit against the AI music generator, warning that its latest AI models could escape scrutiny until at least 2028 if the case is paused, Music Business Worldwide reports. The labels have offered to defer proving ownership of more than 60,000 recordings named in the suit, but they want discovery into how Suno's v6 model was trained to begin immediately. Suno is seeking to put the case on hold, a move the labels argue would let the company keep training and shipping new models while the legal questions sit unanswered. The dispute is one of several major label lawsuits against AI music companies, and it escalated further on Tuesday as Elvis Presley rightsholders amended their own Suno suit to add more than 100 allegedly infringing AI tracks. The outcome matters well beyond Suno: whether AI companies can be forced to disclose their training data — and whether training on copyrighted recordings without a licence is infringement — is the central legal question facing the music industry, and the labels are pushing to keep the pressure on rather than let the cases drift.

articles.title: John Christ, original Danzig guitarist on 'Mother' and more, dead at 61
articles.description: John Christ, the guitarist who played on Danzig's classic early records including 'Mother', has died at 61, Rolling Stone reports. Christ was Danzig's original guitarist, defining the band's heavy blues-metal sound on its first four albums before leaving in 1995. His death was announced on Tuesday.
articles.body: John Christ, the original guitarist of Danzig and the player behind the band's signature heavy blues-metal sound, has died at 61, Rolling Stone reports. Christ joined Glenn Danzig's band at its formation in 1987 and played on its first four albums, including the self-titled debut that produced 'Mother' — the song that became the band's signature hit and a staple of hard-rock radio. His guitar work, blending blues phrasing with crushing metal riffs, helped define Danzig's sound at its commercial peak in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Christ left the band in 1995 after creative and business disputes, and later worked as a session musician and teacher, largely stepping away from the spotlight. His death was announced on Tuesday; no cause was immediately given. He is remembered by fans as the guitarist who gave Danzig its menace and swing — the player whose riffs made 'Mother' one of the most recognisable metal songs of its era.

articles.title: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' sets the all-time Hot 100 record with 28 weeks at No. 1
articles.description: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' has spent a 28th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, making it the longest-running No. 1 single in the chart's 68-year history. It passes Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You', which held the record at 27 weeks on the Streaming Songs chart and 22 weeks at No. 1 overall. Langley's album Dandelion has now also passed Carey's Daydream for the most weeks at No. 1 by a female artist's album.
articles.body: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' has officially become the longest-running No. 1 song in Billboard Hot 100 history, spending a 28th week at the summit on the chart announced Monday, November 16. The country heartbreak anthem, released in October 2025 as the lead single from her album Dandelion, first topped the chart in February 2026 and has dominated through the summer and autumn. It breaks out of a tie with Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' for the most weeks at No. 1 on the Streaming Songs chart, and it also passes Carey's holiday classic as the longest-running No. 1 overall. The achievement is doubly historic for Langley: Dandelion has now surpassed Carey's 1995 album Daydream for the most combined weeks at No. 1 by a female artist's album, with 27 weeks to Daydream's 26. Only 4% of all songs to reach No. 1 in the Hot 100's 67-year history have held the top spot for 10 weeks or more, putting Langley's run in rare company. The song has also earned her seven Grammy nominations, including Record of the Year, announced the same day the record was confirmed.

articles.title: Deutsche Bank moved wealthy Russian clients to Switzerland and Luxembourg before the full-scale war, shielding their records from the DOJ
articles.description: Deutsche Bank began shifting wealthy Russian clients to its divisions in Switzerland and Luxembourg after 2014, Meduza reports, helping shield their financial records from the US Department of Justice. The moves were designed to protect banking secrecy and avoid disclosing information sought by American investigators. The revelations add to the long-running scrutiny of Western banks' handling of Russian money.
articles.body: Deutsche Bank began shifting wealthy Russian clients to its divisions in Switzerland and Luxembourg after 2014, Meduza reports, in moves that helped shield their financial records from the US Department of Justice. The bank used the stricter banking secrecy of its Swiss and Luxembourg arms to avoid disclosing information sought by American investigators probing Russian money flows. The transfers began after Russia's annexation of Crimea and the first round of Western sanctions, and continued in the years before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Deutsche Bank has faced years of scrutiny over its Russian business, including a $630 million fine in 2017 for a mirror-trading scheme that moved billions out of Russia, and questions from US lawmakers about its dealings with Russian clients. The new reporting shows how the bank's structure — with units in jurisdictions with different disclosure rules — could be used to keep sensitive client information out of American investigators' reach. For regulators, it is another reminder of how hard it remains to trace Russian wealth through the Western financial system even after a decade of sanctions.

articles.title: Russian military plane crashes in Kemerovo region, all crew members reportedly killed
articles.description: A Russian military An-12 transport aircraft crashed near the village of Yagunovo in the Kemerovo region, Meduza reports, with all crew members reportedly killed. Russian officials said 17 people died in the crash of the military transport plane. The cause of the crash has not been established.
articles.body: A Russian military An-12 transport aircraft crashed near the village of Yagunovo in the Kemerovo region, Meduza reports, with all crew members reportedly killed. Russian officials said 17 people died in the crash, according to Ukrainska Pravda's account of the Russian statements. The An-12 is a Soviet-era four-engine turboprop that has been in service for decades and is used by the Russian military for cargo and troop transport; the type has a long record of accidents, including several fatal crashes in recent years. The cause of Tuesday's crash has not been established, and Russian authorities have not said what the aircraft was carrying or where it was headed. Military aviation accidents in Russia have become more frequent during the war in Ukraine, as aircraft are flown harder and maintenance strains grow, though there is no indication so far that this crash was connected to the war. Investigators are working at the site, and the Defence Ministry is expected to release more details once the wreckage is examined.

articles.title: Russia's government proposes shielding war participants' property worth up to 10 million rubles from bankruptcy seizure
articles.description: Russia's government has proposed shielding property worth up to 10 million rubles belonging to participants in the war in Ukraine from seizure in bankruptcy proceedings, Meduza reports. The proposal is the latest benefit offered to veterans and their families as the Kremlin tries to keep the war's participants loyal. It would protect homes, savings and other assets from creditors.
articles.body: Russia's government has proposed shielding property worth up to 10 million rubles (roughly $125,000) belonging to participants in the war in Ukraine from seizure in bankruptcy proceedings, Meduza reports. The measure would protect the homes, savings and other assets of veterans and their families from creditors — a significant benefit in a country where the war has driven up debts and financial strain for many households. It is the latest in a long line of perks the Kremlin has offered to those who fought in Ukraine, including mortgage subsidies, free land, priority university places for their children and lump-sum payments for signing up. The benefits serve a dual purpose: they reward service and, just as importantly, they bind veterans and their families to the state, making them a constituency with a direct stake in the war's continuation. The bankruptcy shield also hints at the financial pressure the war is creating at home — wounded veterans, bereaved families and returning soldiers face real economic hardship, and the government is trying to cushion it before discontent grows.

articles.title: Telegram to ban card payments for digital services in-app — with an exception for authoritarian countries
articles.description: Telegram has warned developers of bots and mini-apps that they will only be able to accept payment for digital goods and services through its internal currency, Telegram Stars — bank cards will no longer work inside the app. Founder Pavel Durov later clarified that VPN bots in authoritarian countries will be exempt. The change is driven by Apple and Google rules requiring in-app purchases to go through their own payment systems.
articles.body: Telegram has warned developers of bots and mini-apps that they will soon only be able to accept payment for digital goods and services through its internal currency, Telegram Stars, Meduza reports — bank cards will no longer be accepted for in-app payments. The restrictions are driven by Apple and Google requirements that digital purchases inside apps go through their own payment systems, and Telegram is pushing developers toward Stars as the compliant route. Founder Pavel Durov later clarified that an exception will be made for VPN bots in authoritarian countries, where Stars payments may not be practical or safe for users trying to evade censorship. Durov also noted that users can buy Stars with the cryptocurrency Grams on the Fragment platform. The change matters because Telegram's bot and mini-app ecosystem has become a major economy in its own right — particularly in Russia and Ukraine, where bots handle everything from news to payments to wartime aid. Forcing all of it through Stars gives Telegram a cut of every transaction and tightens its control over the platform, while the VPN exception acknowledges that in some countries the app is a lifeline for circumventing state control.

articles.title: Kremlin says the next US-Russia-Ukraine peace talks will be trilateral, without Europe
articles.description: The Kremlin has said the next round of US-Russia-Ukraine peace talks will be trilateral, with no European participation, Meduza reports. The statement comes days before a separate three-way meeting of Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, and ahead of a Witkoff-Kushner meeting with Ukrainian and European officials in Berlin on November 19. Kyiv and its European partners have insisted they will not accept a deal struck over their heads.
articles.body: The Kremlin has said the next round of US-Russia-Ukraine peace talks will be trilateral, with no European participation, Meduza reports. The announcement sets up a negotiation format that excludes the European governments that have bankrolled much of Ukraine's defence — a format Moscow has long preferred and Kyiv's European partners have long resisted. It comes in a busy diplomatic week: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to meet Ukrainian and European officials in Berlin on November 19, and Donald Trump is set to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen the same day for a first-ever three-way summit focused on nuclear weapons. Meduza also reports an analysis of Russia's clarifying demands for ending the war, with political scientist Alex Yusupov arguing that Putin's maximalist conditions extend beyond Ukraine to the EU, NATO, Finland and Moldova. The trilateral format raises the stakes for Kyiv, which has insisted that no deal can be struck without Ukraine at the table — and Europe, which fears being presented with a fait accompli.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un photographed smoking in an armchair on a ski slope — the perfect meme image
articles.description: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has been photographed sitting in a luxurious armchair directly on a ski slope, cigarette in hand, during a visit to a resort under construction in Samjiyon near the Chinese border. The image, released by state media, has spread widely online as a meme. Kim visited the resort on November 15–16, days before Donald Trump suggested he might meet the North Korean leader during his Asia trip.
articles.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has been photographed sitting in a luxurious armchair placed directly on a ski slope, a cigarette smoking in his hand, during a visit to a resort under construction in Samjiyon, near the Chinese border. The photographs, released by the Korean Central News Agency after Kim's November 15–16 visit, have spread widely online, with the armchair image quickly becoming a meme. The resort is part of Kim's push to develop tourism in the remote northern region, and the staged photo-op — a leader relaxing in comfort on the slopes he is inspecting — is classic North Korean propaganda imagery. The timing is notable: Donald Trump said this week that he might meet Kim during his Asia trip, which takes him to China for a three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Trump and Kim met three times during Trump's first term, and the North Korean leader's carefully choreographed public appearances are often read for signals about his willingness to engage. Whether the ski-slope armchair is one of those signals is anyone's guess — but it is, as Meduza put it, the ideal photograph for memes.

articles.title: Russia's demands for ending the war are clarifying — what does Putin want, and what can he actually get?
articles.description: As US-Russia-Ukraine negotiations intensify, Russia's demands for ending the war are becoming clearer — and they go well beyond Ukraine, Meduza reports in an analysis with political scientist Alex Yusupov. Putin's maximalist conditions touch the EU, NATO, Finland and Moldova, according to the analysis. The piece weighs what Moscow actually wants against what it can realistically extract at the negotiating table.
articles.body: As the negotiating process between Russia and Ukraine intensifies, Moscow's demands for ending the war are becoming clearer — and they extend well beyond Ukraine, Meduza reports in a discussion with political scientist Alex Yusupov, head of the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Russia programme. According to Yusupov, Putin's maximalist conditions touch the European Union, NATO, Finland and Moldova, reflecting a vision of a redrawn European security order rather than a simple territorial settlement in Ukraine. The analysis comes as diplomats publish more insider details about both sides' positions, and as the Kremlin says the next talks will be trilateral — US, Russia and Ukraine — without Europe. Yusupov weighs what Putin actually wants against what he can realistically get: maximalist demands are a familiar opening position, but the gap between them and anything Kyiv or Europe could accept remains enormous. The piece is a useful corrective to the idea that a deal is close — the contours of a settlement are emerging, but so is the scale of the disagreement, and the talks in Berlin and Shenzhen this week will test whether either side is prepared to move.

articles.title: Russia attacks Vinnytsia twice in one day — fire in the city centre, four injured
articles.description: Russian forces attacked Vinnytsia twice on Tuesday, setting a fire in the city centre and injuring four people, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The central Ukrainian city, far from the front line, has been hit repeatedly during the war. The attacks were part of a day of Russian strikes that also hit Dnipro and pushed drones into Moldovan airspace.
articles.body: Russian forces attacked Vinnytsia twice on Tuesday, setting a fire in the city centre and injuring four people, Ukrainska Pravda reports. Vinnytsia, a regional capital in central Ukraine hundreds of kilometres from the front line, has been hit repeatedly during the war, including a devastating missile strike on its centre in July 2022 that killed 27 people. The two attacks on Tuesday continued that pattern of strikes on a city with no direct military significance, and they came on the same day Russian forces hit Dnipro in the evening and sent drones into Moldovan airspace. Four people were injured and a fire broke out in the centre of the city, according to the report. The strikes fit Russia's broader campaign of hitting Ukrainian cities and infrastructure as winter sets in — a campaign the UN says killed at least 372 civilians in October alone, 95% more than a year earlier. For residents of Vinnytsia, the day was a reminder that distance from the front offers no protection.

articles.title: Pistorius: criticise Russian attacks on civilians, not Ukraine's strikes on Russia
articles.description: German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has urged critics of Ukraine's strikes deep inside Russia to focus instead on Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians, Ukrainska Pravda reports. His comments came the same day a deputy to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth condemned Ukraine's deep strikes, saying they 'bring pain to the population'. The contrast highlights a growing transatlantic split over Ukraine's long-range campaign.
articles.body: German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has urged critics of Ukraine's strikes deep inside Russia to focus instead on Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians, Ukrainska Pravda reports. His intervention came on the same day a deputy to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth condemned Ukraine's deep strikes into Russia, saying they 'bring pain to the population' — a striking contrast between the two allies' public positions. Pistorius's argument is that Ukraine's strikes on Russian military and energy targets are a legitimate response to a war of aggression, while Russia's nightly drone and missile barrages deliberately hit Ukrainian cities, hospitals and power plants. The German minister has been one of Ukraine's most consistent backers in Europe, and his comments reflect Berlin's view that Kyiv must be able to hit back at the sources of the attacks it endures. The split matters because the United States is simultaneously pressing Ukraine toward negotiations while questioning one of its main levers — the long-range campaign that has hit Russian refineries, airfields and, this week, the Crimean Bridge. How far Washington will go in restraining Kyiv is now an open question.

articles.title: Hegseth's deputy condemns Ukraine's deep strikes into Russia, saying they 'bring pain to the population'
articles.description: A deputy to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has condemned Ukraine's strikes deep inside Russia, saying they 'bring pain to the population', Ukrainska Pravda reports. The criticism stands in sharp contrast to Germany's defence minister, who on the same day urged critics to focus on Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians instead. The comments suggest Washington is cooling on Kyiv's long-range campaign.
articles.body: A deputy to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has condemned Ukraine's strikes deep inside Russia, saying they 'bring pain to the population', Ukrainska Pravda reports. The criticism is the clearest sign yet that parts of the Trump administration are uncomfortable with Kyiv's long-range campaign against Russian military and energy targets — a campaign that has hit refineries, airfields and, this week, the Crimean Bridge for the second time in two days. The remarks stand in sharp contrast to German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, who on the same day urged critics of Ukraine's strikes to focus instead on Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians. The split between the allies matters because Washington is Ukraine's largest military backer, and any American pressure to curtail the deep-strike campaign would remove one of Kyiv's few ways of imposing costs on Russia directly. It also comes as the administration pushes Ukraine toward negotiations, with envoys Witkoff and Kushner due in Berlin on November 19. Whether the deputy's comments reflect settled administration policy or one official's view is not yet clear — but Kyiv will be watching closely.

articles.title: Britain to give Ukraine more than 1,000 air-defence missiles and radars worth $316 million
articles.description: Britain will supply Ukraine with more than 1,000 air-defence missiles and radars worth $316 million, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The package comes as Russia intensifies its air campaign against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, and as the UN reports a sharp rise in civilian deaths. Air defence remains Kyiv's most urgent request from its partners.
articles.body: Britain will supply Ukraine with more than 1,000 air-defence missiles and radars worth $316 million, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The package is a direct response to Russia's intensifying air campaign against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, which the UN says killed at least 372 civilians in October — 95% more than a year earlier. Air defence has been Kyiv's most urgent request from its partners for months: Russian drone and missile barrages have knocked out power in nine regions, forced emergency outage schedules, and hit targets from the Crimean Bridge to Dnipro and Vinnytsia. Britain has been one of Ukraine's most consistent suppliers of air-defence systems, including Storm Shadow missiles and previous missile packages, and the new delivery adds both interceptors and the radars needed to spot incoming attacks. The announcement lands in the same week that diplomats are pushing toward negotiations in Berlin and Shenzhen — a reminder that, whatever the talks produce, Ukraine's partners are still arming it for the winter ahead.

articles.title: Klitschko: Kyiv partially reopens traffic over the Southern Bridge
articles.description: Kyiv is partially restoring traffic over the Southern Bridge, mayor Vitali Klitschko said — a step toward recovery after Russian strikes on bridges over the Dnipro in the capital. The morning digest reported that Russia had struck bridges in Kyiv, and the partial reopening is the first sign of repair. Public transport has also resumed over the Northern Bridge.
articles.body: Kyiv is partially restoring traffic over the Southern Bridge, mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Tuesday, in the first sign of recovery after Russian strikes on bridges over the Dnipro in the capital. The morning digest reported that Russia had struck bridges in Kyiv, and the Southern Bridge — one of the main crossings linking the two banks of the river — was damaged in the attacks. Public transport has also resumed over the Northern Bridge, according to Ukrainska Pravda, restoring another key link across the city. The bridges are critical infrastructure for a city of nearly three million people, carrying commuters, freight and emergency services between Kyiv's left and right banks. Their targeting is part of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, and the speed of the partial reopening reflects the city's experience in repairing damage under fire. Full restoration will take longer, and the bridges remain vulnerable to further strikes — but for Kyiv residents, the reopening is a tangible sign that the city keeps functioning.

articles.title: Bloomberg: a third of Firaxis Games staff laid off amid XCOM 3 troubles
articles.description: Take-Two Interactive has laid off a third of the staff at Firaxis Games, the studio behind Civilization and XCOM, Bloomberg's Jason Schreier reports — a restructuring tied to problems with XCOM 3. The cuts come just days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, Take-Two's biggest release ever. It is the latest round of layoffs to hit a major strategy studio.
articles.body: Take-Two Interactive has laid off a third of the staff at Firaxis Games, the studio behind Civilization and XCOM, Bloomberg's Jason Schreier reports, in a restructuring tied to problems with the long-awaited XCOM 3. The cuts come just days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, the biggest release in Take-Two's history, and they underline how even a publisher on the verge of a record-breaking launch is trimming elsewhere. Firaxis has been one of the most respected strategy studios in the industry, but its recent output has struggled: Civilization VII, released in 2025, received a mixed reception, and XCOM 3 has reportedly been in troubled development. The layoffs are part of a wider pattern of cuts across the games industry, which has shed tens of thousands of jobs over the past two years even as revenues remain high. For the developers affected, the timing — days before their parent company's biggest ever launch — will sting. For Take-Two, the message is that no studio is safe from restructuring, however storied its name.

articles.title: Skydance cancels Pattinson's Batman Part 3 contract, The Wrap reports
articles.description: Skydance has prematurely cancelled Robert Pattinson's contract for a Batman trilogy — including The Batman: Part 3 — The Wrap reports, according to GameMAG. The news broke in the same week Pattinson was announced as the next James Bond. Production on The Batman: Part 2 has stalled for years, and director Matt Reeves has reportedly been replaced by Steven Soderbergh.
articles.body: Skydance has prematurely cancelled Robert Pattinson's contract for a trilogy of Batman films, including The Batman: Part 3, The Wrap reports, according to GameMAG. The news broke in the same week that Amazon announced Pattinson as the next James Bond — a coincidence that looks less coincidental by the hour. Production on The Batman: Part 2 has stalled for years, and GameMAG reports that director Matt Reeves has been replaced by Steven Soderbergh, a sign of how troubled the sequel has become. The cancellation fits a broader upheaval at DC: studio chiefs James Gunn and Peter Safran were fired, and Skydance is reportedly bracing for the failure of the Superman sequel starring Nicholas Hoult — the other actor who screen-tested for Bond. For Pattinson, the Bond announcement softens the blow considerably: he trades a stalled superhero franchise for the most famous role in cinema. For DC, it is another sign that its film universe is being rebuilt from scratch, with even its biggest stars moving on.

articles.title: Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic news coming in early 2027, Casey Hudson says
articles.description: New details about Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic will start emerging in early 2027, project lead Casey Hudson — creator of the original Knights of the Old Republic — said in a podcast. Development is moving fast, according to Hudson. The game, from veterans of BioWare, is one of the most anticipated Star Wars titles in years.
articles.body: New details about Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic will start emerging in early 2027, project lead Casey Hudson said in a podcast, GameMAG reports. Hudson, the creator of the original Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, said development is moving fast — encouraging news for a project that has been largely silent since its announcement. The game is being made by a team of BioWare veterans, and it carries the weight of one of the most beloved Star Wars games ever made: the 2003 Knights of the Old Republic is still regarded as one of the greatest RPGs of all time, and its story of Revan remains a touchstone for fans. Fate of the Old Republic is expected to return to that era of the Old Republic, thousands of years before the films, though Hudson has not confirmed the setting. The early-2027 reveal window gives fans a date to circle, and it suggests the game is further along than many assumed. For Star Wars gaming, which has had a mixed decade, a confident, well-made Old Republic game would be a major event.

articles.title: The Witcher 4 developers promise to keep the soul of The Witcher
articles.description: The Witcher 4 developers have promised to preserve 'the soul and heart' of The Witcher in the new game, GameMAG reports. The game just won Most Anticipated Game at the Golden Joystick Awards 2026, voted by players worldwide. CD Projekt RED has said little about the sequel, which stars Ciri as its protagonist.
articles.body: The developers of The Witcher 4 have promised to preserve 'the soul and heart' of The Witcher in the new game, GameMAG reports. The reassurance comes as the game won Most Anticipated Game at the Golden Joystick Awards 2026, a prize voted by players around the world — a sign of how much expectation is riding on CD Projekt RED's next RPG. The Witcher 4 will star Ciri as its protagonist, a major shift from Geralt, who anchored the first three games and the Netflix series. That change has prompted questions from fans about whether the new game will still feel like The Witcher, and the developers' comments are aimed squarely at those doubts. CD Projekt RED has released little concrete detail about the game so far, beyond early trailers, and no release date has been announced. The Golden Joystick win underlines the scale of the anticipation — and the risk. The Witcher 3 is widely regarded as one of the greatest games ever made, and its successor will be judged against it from the moment it is shown.

articles.title: Xbox Project Helix is a console, not a PC, Microsoft says
articles.description: Microsoft's next-generation Xbox, codenamed Project Helix, is first and foremost a console that will also be able to run PC games, Xbox lead engineer Jason Ronald has revealed. The clarification, in a digital magazine marking 25 years of the Xbox brand, settles months of speculation about whether Microsoft's next machine would effectively be a PC. The news follows Shift Up's interest in developing for Helix.
articles.body: Microsoft's next-generation Xbox, codenamed Project Helix, is being developed first and foremost as a console that will also be able to run PC games, Xbox lead engineer Jason Ronald has revealed, GameMAG reports. The clarification, given in a digital magazine marking 25 years of the Xbox brand, settles months of speculation about whether Microsoft's next machine would effectively be a gaming PC in a console box. Ronald's framing — a console first, with PC compatibility — suggests Microsoft wants to keep the simplicity of console gaming while opening the door to the vast PC library. The news comes days after Stellar Blade developer Shift Up said it was interested in making games for Xbox and had its eye on Project Helix, with its technical director saying the studio hoped to be among the first to receive next-generation dev kits. Microsoft has not announced a release date for Helix, but the steady flow of detail suggests the reveal is approaching. For players, the key question is what 'runs PC games' means in practice — and whether Helix will finally blur the line between console and PC for good.

articles.title: FEMA's emergency alert test went smoothly, officials say
articles.description: The Trump administration conducted a routine nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System on Tuesday, and officials say it went smoothly.
