The company buys, manages and markets music rights, earning revenue from streaming, licensing and other uses, with a strategy focused largely on independent musicians and artists with established regional audiences. The raise shows how aggressively institutional money is moving into music royalties as an asset class, with competition for valuable song rights intensifying.

articles.title: HYBE, home to BTS and KATSEYE, forms a strategic partnership with CAA
articles.description: HYBE and Creative Artists Agency have formed a strategic partnership, announced on Monday, to expand the reach of HYBE’s artists, intellectual property and brands. The companies will work together on brand partnerships, live experiences, licensing, merchandising, sports and content. The deal follows HYBE’s record-breaking third quarter, driven largely by BTS’ return.
articles.body: HYBE, the South Korean entertainment group behind BTS, KATSEYE, ENHYPEN and SEVENTEEN, has formed a strategic partnership with Creative Artists Agency, the companies announced on Monday. Through the deal, HYBE aims to increase the reach of its artists, intellectual property and brands, with the two companies collaborating on brand partnerships, live experiences, licensing and merchandising, sports and content across markets HYBE dominates, including Korea, Japan, China, India and the Americas. HYBE CEO Jason Jaesang Lee said the partnership would help the company grow its global commercial footprint. The deal follows closely on HYBE’s record-breaking third quarter, largely driven by BTS’ return: the company reported revenue of 1.5257 trillion Korean won, about $1.135 billion. The partnership pairs one of the world’s biggest music companies with one of Hollywood’s most powerful agencies, and it signals how K-pop’s biggest player plans to convert its artists’ popularity into a broader entertainment and lifestyle business.

articles.title: TuneCore names Tash Shah as global marketing VP to lead brand strategy
articles.description: TuneCore has appointed Tash Shah as vice president of global marketing, tasking her with building brand strategy, creative direction and product marketing campaigns across all markets. She takes the role effective immediately. The appointment comes as the digital distribution space consolidates, with TuneCore competing against DistroKid, CD Baby and others.
articles.body: TuneCore has appointed Tash Shah as vice president, global marketing, tasking her with building brand strategy, creative direction and product marketing campaigns across all markets, Music Business Worldwide reported. Shah takes the role effective immediately and reports to senior leadership. The appointment follows a period of consolidation in the digital music distribution space, where TuneCore competes with DistroKid, CD Baby and a growing field of rivals that handle metadata, royalty collection and artist services for independent musicians and labels. For independent artists, the distributor they choose is increasingly a strategic decision: it determines how their music reaches streaming services, how quickly they are paid and what tools they get to grow. TuneCore does not disclose quarterly earnings or revenue figures, so the company’s growth rate is not public, but the senior marketing hire signals investment in customer lifecycle and creative positioning.

articles.title: Az Cohen’s AZTEC, a joint venture label with Believe, has signed its first artist
articles.description: AZTEC, the joint venture label launched by Az Cohen with Believe, has signed its first artist. Believe unveiled AZTEC in May, describing it as its first joint venture in the United States. The signing is the first test of a model that pairs an independent label operator with a global distribution and services company.
articles.body: Az Cohen’s AZTEC, a joint venture label with Believe, has signed its first artist, Music Business Worldwide reported. Believe unveiled AZTEC in May, describing it as its first joint venture in the United States, and the first signing is the label’s first public test. The model pairs an independent label operator’s A&R instincts with a global company’s distribution, marketing and services infrastructure, a structure that has become increasingly common as the major-label system fragments. For Believe, which has built its business on serving independent labels and artists, the venture is a way to move further into frontline A&R in the world’s biggest music market. The identity of the first signing and the terms of the deal have not been disclosed in detail, but the announcement marks AZTEC’s formal arrival as a working label rather than a press-release concept.

articles.title: Beyoncé becomes the first artist ever to earn 100 Grammy nominations
articles.description: Beyoncé made history as the first artist ever to earn 100 Grammy Award nominations, with the 2027 nominations announced on Monday. She leads a field that also has Raye, Rosalía and Ella Langley among the top nominees. The milestone extends a record she already held as the most decorated artist in Grammys history.
articles.body: The 2027 Grammy nominations were announced on Monday, and Beyoncé reached 100 career nominations — the first artist in the awards’ history to do so. She was already the most awarded artist in Grammy history, and the new total cements a lead no other performer has approached. Raye, Rosalía and Ella Langley are among the leading nominees this year, while the nominations also produced some of the most talked-about snubs in years: Harry Styles was blanked entirely, and BTS were not nominated. Dolly Parton competes against herself in one of the country categories, and Miley Cyrus earned a nomination alongside her godmother Parton. The nominations set up a wide-open race, with the country categories drawing particular attention for an odd gender split — women dominate the contemporary categories while men dominate the traditional ones. The ceremony itself is still to come, but the nomination morning already delivered the year’s biggest music story.

articles.title: Raye, Rosalía and Ella Langley lead the 2027 Grammy nominees
articles.description: Raye, Rosalía and Ella Langley lead the nominees for the 2027 Grammy Awards, announced on Monday. Beyoncé made history as the first artist to reach 100 career nominations. The nominations also delivered some of the year’s biggest snubs, with Harry Styles blanked and BTS left out entirely.
articles.body: Raye, Rosalía and Ella Langley lead the nominees for the 2027 Grammy Awards, Rolling Stone reported, after the nominations were announced on Monday. The three artists sit at the top of a field that also gave Beyoncé her 100th career nomination — the first artist ever to reach that total. The nominations reflect a year in which pop, Latin music and country all produced defining records, with Rosalía’s third Album of the Year win at the Latin Grammys still fresh in the memory. But the morning also produced the year’s most argued-over snubs: Harry Styles was blanked entirely, BTS were not nominated, and the country categories drew attention for an odd gender split, with women dominating the contemporary categories and men the traditional ones. Dolly Parton competes against herself in one country category. The nominations set up a wide-open race, and the snubs and surprises — rather than the favourites — dominated the first day of conversation.

articles.title: The Grammy nominations blanked Harry Styles. What happened?
articles.description: Harry Styles received no nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, one of the biggest surprises of nomination morning. Rolling Stone asks what happened to one of pop’s biggest stars. The snub stands in contrast to a field led by Raye, Rosalía, Ella Langley and a history-making Beyoncé.
articles.body: The 2027 Grammy nominations blanked Harry Styles entirely, Rolling Stone reported, in one of the biggest surprises of nomination morning. Styles, one of the defining pop stars of the past decade, received no nominations at all, and the magazine asks what happened. The snub is striking because the field is otherwise wide open, with Raye, Rosalía and Ella Langley leading the nominees and Beyoncé making history with her 100th career nomination. Grammy voters have a long record of unpredictable choices, and the snub will fuel the annual debate about whether the awards reflect the year in music or the industry’s internal politics. For Styles, the blank is a reminder that even the biggest stars are not guaranteed a place on the ballot, and it leaves his fans — and the wider pop world — waiting to see whether he responds with new music or simply lets the moment pass.

articles.title: Don’t be surprised that BTS aren’t nominated for the 2027 Grammys
articles.description: BTS were not nominated for the 2027 Grammy Awards, and Rolling Stone argues the snub should not surprise anyone. The group’s return drove HYBE to a record-breaking quarter, but Grammy voters have repeatedly overlooked K-pop’s biggest act. The piece examines why the world’s biggest band keeps missing out.
articles.body: BTS were not nominated for the 2027 Grammy Awards, and Rolling Stone argues that nobody should be surprised. The group’s return drove HYBE to a record-breaking third quarter, with revenue of about $1.135 billion, and they remain the biggest band in the world by most measures. But Grammy voters have repeatedly overlooked K-pop’s biggest act, and the 2027 ballot is no exception. The piece examines the structural reasons: the Grammys have historically been slow to recognise music made outside the Anglo-American mainstream, and K-pop’s fan-driven, multi-format model does not map neatly onto the Recording Academy’s categories. The snub also stands in contrast to the Latin Grammys, where Rosalía made history with a third Album of the Year win. For BTS and their fans, the omission is familiar rather than shocking — and it raises the question of whether the Grammys or the band need each other more.

articles.title: Lawsuit accusing Selena Gomez and Wondermind co-founders of fraud is dismissed
articles.description: A lawsuit accusing Selena Gomez and the co-founders of her mental-health startup Wondermind of fraud has been dismissed. Billboard also reported that Gomez is no longer facing the suit. The dismissal closes a legal cloud over the singer’s wellness venture.
articles.body: A lawsuit accusing Selena Gomez and the co-founders of her mental-health startup Wondermind of fraud has been dismissed, Rolling Stone reported. The case had cast a legal cloud over Gomez’s wellness venture, which she launched as an extension of her public advocacy around mental health. Billboard separately reported that Gomez is no longer facing the lawsuit, confirming the dismissal from the music industry’s side. The details of the ruling have not been fully disclosed, but the dismissal removes a significant distraction for Gomez, who remains one of the most commercially powerful figures in pop. Wondermind was an unusual venture for a pop star — a media and wellness company built around mental-health content — and the lawsuit had raised questions about its governance and finances. With the case dismissed, the company can move forward without the litigation hanging over it.

articles.title: Stephen Wilson Jr. announces a double album and unveils a stunning ‘I’m a Song’ with Chris Stapleton
articles.description: Stephen Wilson Jr. has announced a double album, Impressiøn of a Human // Children of the Cørnerman, due in February, and shared a new song, ‘I’m a Song,’ with Chris Stapleton. Wilson Jr. performed an acoustic ‘Wonderwall’ as a tribute to Oasis at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony at the weekend.
articles.body: Stephen Wilson Jr. has announced a double album, Impressiøn of a Human // Children of the Cørnerman, due for release in February, and unveiled a new song, ‘I’m a Song,’ featuring Chris Stapleton. The collaboration pairs Wilson Jr.’s outlaw-country songwriting with Stapleton’s powerhouse voice, and Rolling Stone calls the track stunning. The announcement caps a big week for Wilson Jr., who performed an acoustic version of ‘Wonderwall’ as a tribute to Oasis at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony at the weekend. The double album is an ambitious statement from an artist who has built a following on the strength of his songwriting rather than hit singles, and the Stapleton collaboration signals the regard in which he is held by Nashville’s biggest names. February’s release will be one of the first major country records of 2027.

articles.title: Miley Cyrus shares a sweet memory of godmother Dolly Parton as they earn a Grammy nod together
articles.description: Miley Cyrus has shared a sweet memory of her godmother Dolly Parton as the two earned a Grammy nomination together. Parton also competes against herself in one of the 2027 Grammys’ country categories. The pair’s collaboration is one of the feel-good stories of nomination morning.
articles.body: Miley Cyrus has shared a sweet memory of her godmother Dolly Parton as the two earned a Grammy nomination together, Rolling Stone reported. The joint nod is one of the feel-good stories of nomination morning, pairing one of pop’s biggest stars with her godmother, one of country music’s most beloved figures. Parton also competes against herself in one of the 2027 Grammys’ country categories, a quirk that underlines how prolific she remains. The nomination comes as the pair’s work together continues to resonate: Parton’s collaboration with U2 on “Torn” won Billboard’s fan-voted favourite new music poll this week. For Cyrus, the shared nomination is a reminder of a relationship that has shaped her career, from her childhood in Parton’s orbit to her own stardom. It is also a rare moment of warmth in a nominations morning dominated by snubs and surprises.

articles.title: Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” re-enters the Hot 100 top 10 as Karol G and Ariana Grande climb
articles.description: Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” re-enters the top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100 on the chart dated November 21, while Karol G and Ariana Grande also climb. Tame Impala’s “Dracula” featuring Blackpink’s Jennie holds at No. 3 for a second week. The new chart will be posted in full on Billboard’s website on November 17.
articles.body: Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” is back in the top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100 on the chart dated November 21, 2026, with Karol G and Ariana Grande also rising — and Billboard is teasing the question of whether either can take the No. 1 spot. Tame Impala’s “Dracula,” featuring Blackpink’s Jennie, held at No. 3 on the Hot 100 for a second consecutive week, matching its peak. The track also topped the multimetric Hot Dance/Electronic Songs chart for a 45th week and the Hot Rock & Alternative Songs chart for a 26th week, and extended its run atop the Radio Songs chart to a ninth week. On Billboard’s global charts, Tate McRae’s “Housewife” and Karol G’s “BbY WOW,” featuring Judeline and Rusowsky, lead the way for the week dated November 21, underlining how international hits continue to dominate worldwide streaming. The full new Hot 100 will be posted on Billboard’s website on November 17.

articles.title: Tame Impala and Blackpink’s Jennie hold No. 3 on the Hot 100 with ‘Dracula’
articles.description: Tame Impala’s “Dracula,” featuring Blackpink’s Jennie, held at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 for a second consecutive week, matching its peak. The track also topped the Hot Dance/Electronic Songs chart for a 45th week and the Hot Rock & Alternative Songs chart for a 26th week. It extended its run atop the Radio Songs chart to a ninth week.
articles.body: Tame Impala and Blackpink’s Jennie held at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 with “Dracula,” matching the track’s peak for a second straight week, according to a chart preview. The song also topped the multimetric Hot Dance/Electronic Songs chart for a 45th week and the Hot Rock & Alternative Songs chart for a 26th week, and it extended its chart-topping run on the Radio Songs chart to a ninth week. The collaboration has been one of the year’s most durable hits, crossing genre lines in a way few records manage: it is simultaneously a dance record, a rock record and a pop record, depending on which chart you look at. For Jennie, the run adds to a remarkable year for Blackpink’s members as solo artists, and for Tame Impala it confirms the project’s move from psych-rock cult act to mainstream chart force. The full Hot 100 will be posted on Billboard’s website on November 17.

articles.title: Tate McRae and Karol G lead Billboard’s Global charts as international hits gain momentum
articles.description: Tate McRae and Karol G lead Billboard’s Global charts for the week dated November 21, as international hits continue to gain momentum. McRae’s “Housewife” and Karol G’s “BbY WOW,” featuring Judeline and Rusowsky, are among the leading songs reaching audiences across international markets. The two charts measure streaming and sales in more than 200 territories.
articles.body: Tate McRae and Karol G continue to make their mark on the international music charts, leading Billboard’s Global charts for the week dated November 21. McRae’s “Housewife” has enjoyed continued success since its October release, and the Canadian singer previously topped both the Billboard Global 200 and Global Excl. US charts with the single, adding to her earlier chart success with “Greedy.” Karol G’s “BbY WOW,” featuring Judeline and Rusowsky, previously spent six weeks at No. 1 on both global rankings, demonstrating its reach across international markets. The two Billboard charts measure streaming and digital song sales across more than 200 territories; the Global 200 includes the United States, while the Global Excl. US ranking focuses on activity outside the country. The results underline how the centre of gravity in pop has shifted: the biggest songs in the world are increasingly not American records, and the global charts are where that shift is most visible.

articles.title: Wale on his pair of 2027 Grammy nominations: ‘I hope it teaches a lot of people about resilience’
articles.description: Wale has earned a pair of nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards for his album Everything Is a Lot, and he told Billboard he hopes the recognition “teaches a lot of people about resilience.” The nominations cap a long career in which the rapper has been more respected than rewarded. He is one of the feel-good stories of nomination morning.
articles.body: Wale has earned a triumphant pair of nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards for Everything Is a Lot, Billboard reported, and the rapper said he hopes the recognition “teaches a lot of people about resilience.” The nominations cap a long career in which Wale has been more respected by his peers than rewarded by the industry’s biggest prizes. Everything Is a Lot is the latest in a run of records that have kept him relevant across nearly two decades in hip-hop, a longevity few of his contemporaries can match. The nominations come in a year when the Grammys’ rap categories are among the most competitive, and Wale’s inclusion is one of the feel-good stories of nomination morning. For an artist who has spoken openly about the ups and downs of his career, the recognition is a validation of persistence — and, as he put it, a lesson in resilience.

articles.title: Music Victoria goes blunt in its election fight for music funding
articles.description: Music Victoria, the peak body for music in the Australian state, has gone blunt in its election fight for music funding. The organisation is pressing political parties to commit to support for the live music sector. It is the latest sign of how tightly funding and politics are now bound up in the music business.
articles.body: Music Victoria has gone blunt in its election fight for music funding, Billboard reported, pressing political parties in the Australian state to commit to support for the live music sector. The peak body’s unusually direct campaigning reflects how precarious the economics of live music have become, with venues closing, costs rising and audiences squeezed. The fight is the latest sign of how tightly funding and politics are now bound up in the music business, from state-level grants in Australia to the arguments over streaming economics and AI in the US and Europe. Music Victoria’s stance is also a reminder that the industry’s biggest debates are not only about stars and charts: for most working musicians, the question is whether the venues, grants and infrastructure that sustain a scene will survive. The outcome of the election will determine how much support the sector can expect.

articles.title: In the Wake of the 2026 Midterms, Can We Reframe the Patriotic Song?
articles.author: Marissa R. Moss
articles.description: Country artists like Brandy Clark, Mickey Guyton and the War and Treaty are trying to take the patriotic song — and the flag — back from partisan politics after the midterms, and this is the sharpest account of how they're doing it.
articles.body:
When Brandy Clark arrived on set to film the lyric video for her new single "American Roots," her makeup artist had an idea: paint her face and hands red, white and blue, riffing on the song's vision of a loving, inclusive America where everyone, including immigrants, belongs. Clark was nervous at first. As she tells Rolling Stone, "I'm so associated with the rainbow flag... But we deserve this. My fans deserve to see this. And a lot of people in my family, my dad being one of them, served in the military for that flag. That's all of our flag. MAGA does not own the flag." The piece opens on that image and asks the question of the moment: after a November midterm in which a blue wave delivered Democratic gains in states once dismissed as lost causes — taking both the House and the Senate — can artists change their relationship to the patriotic song?

The argument is that the flag and the patriotic song were captured twice over: first by the Trump administration, which has worked to turn the flag into a symbol of exclusion rather than pride, and earlier by a post-9/11 country-radio landscape in which jingoistic songs passing as patriotism became radio gold. Clark's answer is a gentle one. "American Roots," written with Michael Pollack and Griff Clawson and drawing on Woody Guthrie's "This Land Is Your Land," insists that we are all Americans with equal rights to walk on hallowed land, wherever we came from. Its bridge carries the thesis: "When you set foot onto that shore, it's no more mine than it is yours." Clark describes the song as a conversation between two people who might not agree — an attempt to find commonality first, so that even a listener who disagrees might hear the bridge and find something of themselves in it.

She is not alone. Mickey Guyton was already pushing the same idea in 2021 on "All American" from her debut album Remember Her Name — "We got the same stars, the same stripes, just wanna live that good life... Ain't we all all-American?" — a song the piece notes would have been a radio hit sung by a white conservative man, but which from Guyton changes the definition of who gets to own a patriotic song. The War and Treaty's Michael Trotter Jr., a combat veteran of the Iraq war, frames the work as divorcing patriotism from partisan and often hateful politics: "I take great pride in being able to say that I served this country and served it well... So, I am ashamed that people would hide behind the term 'patriotism.'" The piece contrasts that with Zac Brown's claim that performing the National Anthem at President Trump's UFC match on the White House lawn was "patriotism, not politics" — hard to square, it notes, with sharing a stage where a fighter later celebrated by shouting "Michelle Obama is a man." Sheryl Crow adds that words like "patriotic" and "patriot" are used to create sides: "I feel very patriotic about my country, but I'm not a conservative... [patriotic] is used for one category of people and it's used against others and I take offense with that."

The piece closes with a viral clip from the Newport Folk Festival, where Joan Baez — alongside Mavis Staples, Nathaniel Rateliff, Brandi Carlile and others — closed the festival with "America the Beautiful," introducing it with the words "This song is something that we are taking back." Whether the midterm results will embolden more artists to reclaim their version of a patriotic anthem is still an open question, the piece concludes, "but with songs like 'American Roots,' the tide seems to be turning. Everyone should get to partake in this musical tradition, regardless of political beliefs." Clark, whose album The Bird is out in January, puts it simply: "I'm a proud American. Why can't I be patriotic by saying we all belong?"

articles.title: An 'America First' Approach to Famine
articles.author: Hana Kiros
articles.description: For the first time since the 1980s, the US is facing a famine warning and doing nothing — this is the definitive reporting on how that decision was made, and what it is already costing in Somalia.
articles.body:
The piece opens in 1967, when two former State Department employees, William and Paul Paddock, published the bestselling book Famine—1975!, arguing that the United States should reject what they called the "brand-new obligation to feed the world's hungry" — in their vision, the countries that grew wheat would rule, and America could be as great as Athens or Byzantium if it let go of feeding the world. Their projections turned out to be exceptionally wrong: the global population doubled, catastrophic famines became far rarer thanks to agricultural innovation and political will, and the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS Net), created under Ronald Reagan, learned to forecast hunger emergencies months in advance. Whenever FEWS Net assessed a credible risk of famine, Republican and Democratic presidents alike sent food and basic medicines to try to minimize deaths.

That consensus has now broken. FEWS Net is warning about a rising possibility of famine in Somalia, and for the first time since the 1980s the US government, faced with this kind of disaster, has done nothing and apparently plans to continue doing nothing. In Somalia, back-to-back droughts that began last year have killed more than one million livestock. Most Somalis are goat, sheep and camel herders who cannot expect help from a government that is corrupt and devotes most of its small budget to fighting al-Shabaab, al-Qaeda's Somali affiliate, which controls a third of the country and has let major irrigation projects fall into disrepair. International assistance is newly scarce or nonexistent. Half a million children now have severe acute malnutrition, the last stage of hunger before death, and Somalia's emergency-management agency predicts that, thanks in large part to the Super El Niño, the coming months may bring the worst flash floods the country has seen this century — drowning crops and animals and cutting off the humanitarian workers who remain.

The numbers tell the story of the reversal. The peak of humanitarian funding to Somalia came in 2022, when the Biden administration, with Congress's approval, spent more than $2 billion to prevent a catastrophic famine that FEWS Net said was possible; researchers later estimated that American aid alone saved about 3 million lives across East Africa. In recent years the US sent an average of $450 million a year to Somalia. In 2025, President Trump sent a quarter of that amount. This fiscal year, despite a similarly dire forecast, the US is allocating zero dollars. In January, the State Department announced in a social-media post that it was pausing all foreign assistance to Somalia, alleging the country had wasted American resources. The stated reason: the Somali government, while redeveloping a port area, had destroyed a warehouse containing 83 tons of fortified foods partly paid for by the United States — though the World Food Programme's second-in-command, Carl Skau, told Kiros the organization ultimately recovered all of the food. A State Department spokesperson, writing from a shared email account and declining to be named, said only that "The Trump Administration maintains a firm zero tolerance policy for waste, theft, or diversion of U.S. resources."

But Kiros reports the decision may have been made weeks before the warehouse demolition. According to an internal document she reviewed, in November of last year the State Department was considering distributing foreign assistance to Somalia; a plan was drawn up, then abruptly, on December 1, a senior leader told the people who had worked on it to prepare for no funds to be sent at all. The timing followed a New York Times investigation that found Medicaid fraud orchestrated by dozens of members of Minnesota's Somali diaspora, after which the president railed against the Somali American community — at a livestreamed Cabinet meeting on December 2, he said Somali Americans "come from hell," "do nothing but bitch," and should "go back to where they came from and fix it." Asked whether the president's animosity contributed to the decision, the spokesperson declined to answer, saying only that "The United States is not responsible for providing every country in the world the resources to respond to their own domestic situations."

The consequences are already visible: FEWS Net pointed to "historically low and declining levels of humanitarian assistance" as a factor in its first famine warning; other countries have also pulled back; since last year, 205 health and nutrition facilities in Somalia have shut down and hundreds more have scaled back or may soon close. The war in Iran has sent the cost of food, fuel and fertilizer skyrocketing — the price of a single carton of therapeutic peanut paste, the fortified treatment for children too weak from malnutrition to digest food, has quadrupled, as has the price of clean water. The administration has also made it harder for Somali Americans to send money home to relatives, a revenue stream that normally exceeds all humanitarian assistance to the country. Meanwhile the machinery of warning itself has been degraded: the FEWS Net website went dark for half of last year as USAID was dismantled, and although the program was reestablished under the State Department, this summer it stopped publishing hunger forecasts for Somalia, Afghanistan and Yemen, resuming them only in September after backlash from experts and the old humanitarian guard. The State Department's current strategic plan states that "globalist or humanitarian bases" won't guide where lifesaving aid is sent — politics will — and Food for Peace, the federal program that sends American-grown surplus produce abroad, has been revised to exclude many majority-Muslim countries, including Somalia. The administration's legally required plan for combating global hunger is more than a month overdue.

The piece closes with a precedent from 1985, when Peter McPherson, the head of USAID under Reagan and the architect of FEWS Net, brought photos of skeletal Ethiopian children to the Oval Office, leading Reagan to declare that "a hungry child knows no politics" and help the country through a famine despite its Marxist dictator. McPherson told Kiros he believes Trump will be moved to reconsider helping Somalia when similar pictures appear on the nightly news. "Of course, by then, many people will have died," he said. The Paddock brothers' apocalyptic vision may never have come to pass — but half a century later, their argument against feeding the hungry has a new life.

articles.title: Those forced to cross borders are imagining a radical new world
articles.author: Shahram Khosravi
articles.description: A scholar who was once jailed at nineteen for crossing a border argues that the people states call fugitives are really architects of other possible worlds — a big, humane essay that runs from Douglass to Gaza to Kabul.
articles.body:
The essay opens in 1986, when the author was nineteen and behind bars in a small prison on the Iran-Pakistan border, arrested while attempting to cross irregularly into Pakistan. The cells held an extraordinary diversity of people — local smugglers, large-scale drug traffickers, undocumented migrant workers and refugees; Iranians, Afghans, Pakistanis, and Baluch men whose communities had crossed these lands freely for generations but were now punished for violating the territorial order of the nation-state. They all shared one thing: they had refused, for different reasons, to respect the border. The state saw them through a single imaginary, as criminals, trespassers, illegal bodies to be contained. They, however, were animated by different imaginations — each had imagined a life that exceeded the border and acted on it. The prison, he writes, became the most important school of border studies he ever attended: conversations in the cells and the yard revolved around how borders operate, how they are enforced, and above all how they might be circumvented. It was an unlikely site of knowledge production — not just survival strategies, but the enactment of an imagination that paid no heed to prison walls.

That insight frames the essay's central idea: the fugitive imagination. Years later, in a prison north of Stockholm, Khosravi interviewed a human smuggler who described himself as an architect — "I design a journey, like an architect designs a building." Architects imagine structures that do not yet exist; smugglers, likewise, design border crossings that from the state's perspective would be impossible, imagining routes where borders appear closed and connections where states impose separation. Fugitivity and imagination are oriented toward the future, toward not-yet-realised possibilities, while state power relies on backward-looking imaginaries grounded in myths of shared blood, origin and belonging. States treat imagination as a threat precisely because it exposes borders as political constructions that can be reimagined, negotiated and crossed — like capitalism, the nation-state depends on such imaginaries to stabilise its claims to totality.

The history of fugitivity, he argues, is entangled with the history of modernity itself — a modernity grounded in racial capitalism and constituted through colonialism and the nation-state. The continuity runs from enslaved people fleeing plantations to refugees crossing contemporary borders; indeed, "refugee" and "fugitive" share the same etymological root in the Latin fugere, to flee. The essay lingers on Frederick Douglass, whose enslaver Hugh Auld forbade him to learn to read, declaring that if Douglass learned to read, "there would be no keeping him" — he would inevitably desire to write, and "this accomplished, he will be running away with himself." To run away with oneself is not simply to flee physically; it is to reclaim imagination and humanity. Under slavery, where Black bodies were turned into capital, fugitivity was criminalised as theft — the fugitive was pursued because he was perceived to have stolen property from his enslaver: his own body. Literacy was inseparable from emancipation, and pedagogy itself became fugitive, practised under conditions of flight and opacity. The historian Jarvis Givens traces this criminalised Black education in Fugitive Pedagogy, and the struggle did not end with slavery: it continued through Jim Crow and into the present, where attacks on Black studies and critical race theory are the latest hostility toward knowledge that exposes structures of racial subordination.

The same logic operates today. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations to arrest undocumented migrants are often conducted near schools, deterring parents from sending children for fear of detention; a study of five California school districts found a 22 per cent increase in daily student absences following ICE raids in early 2025. In Europe, universities are shaped by hostile climates in which curricula are regulated and critical fields delegitimised; Sweden proposed a law requiring state employees, including teachers and professors, to report undocumented migrants to the police — amended after protests to exclude teachers and doctors, though tax officers and insurance agents must still "snitch." Palestine offers the starkest example: resistance is sustained by a fugitive imagination of freedom beyond colonial domination, and Israel's imposition of its colonial imaginary targets not only bodies and institutions but the spaces where alternative futures are imagined — "scholasticide," the systematic destruction of educational institutions. Since the start of the recent war in Gaza, more than 95 per cent of schools have been damaged or destroyed, disrupting the education of nearly 700,000 students, and all 19 of Gaza's recognised higher education institutions, including 12 universities, have been destroyed, with approximately 100 professors killed. The pattern is old: Birzeit University was shut down 15 times between 1973 and 1992, including a closure of almost four and a half years, and underground "cells of illegal education" were raided, their equipment smashed. Yet the suppression generated fugitive pedagogy — teaching moved into homes, churches and mosques.

Afghanistan shows the same dynamic shaped by gender rather than race. Since the Taliban regained control in August 2021, they have systematically restricted women and girls, banning them from secondary schools and universities in March 2022; by August 2025 nearly 2.2 million Afghan girls were barred from education beyond the primary level. Underground schools have emerged in living rooms, basements and private halls in Kabul. What the Taliban fear, Khosravi writes, is not women's education but the fugitive imagination it cultivates — literacy transforms consciousness and enables women to refuse the patriarchal imaginary, echoing Auld's warning that an enslaved person who learned to read would become "unmanageable." The Moria camp on Lesvos, set up in January 2013 and once Europe's largest and most notorious refugee camp, offers another case: its harsh militarised regulation produced a "camp imaginary" positioning refugees as unwanted, unfree and disposable, yet refugees created alternative spaces of learning, artistic expression and collective care — through education, music, art and everyday mutual support they generated the conditions for survival. The camp burned down in 2020, but many former residents became filmmakers, musicians, poets, researchers and activists, demonstrating that while the camp sought to contain people physically, it could not extinguish their capacity to imagine otherwise.

Drawing on the Chicana scholar Gloria Anzaldúa's concept of "borderland thinking," Khosravi describes the fugitive imagination as situated knowledge produced by people who must survive systems of capture, confinement and bordering — Anzaldúa's la facultad, the capacity to see in surface phenomena the meaning of deeper realities, developed as a survival skill on the US-Mexico border. To gain access to imagination is to break with the imaginaries that make every future appear the same; politics is not only a struggle over power but a struggle over images, imaginaries and imagination itself — a battle over what can be thought, desired and made possible. The essay closes on a personal note: earlier this year, Khosravi received a WhatsApp call from a childhood friend in Iran, the first call from there in more than three months, after protests that began in December 2025 were violently suppressed, thousands killed, and telecommunications cut — followed by an intense US-Israel war with Iran that began on the last day of February 2026. Through a fragmented connection, his friend spoke of spring bringing abundant rain. Khosravi imagined mountains saturated with water, springs running full, wheat fields nourished and waiting to be harvested. To look toward the sky and see rain falling alongside bombs was a refusal of the imperial imaginary — an imagination of life, despite everything, that cannot be killed, bombed, stolen or abducted, and from which the seeds of an alternative future might emerge. From the plantation to the border, from Palestine to the Taliban's war on women, from refugee camps to the war on Iran, attempts to preserve regimes of truth continually generate their own negation. "This is why history never ends."

articles.title: China confirms Xi will host Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on November 19
articles.description: China's foreign ministry has officially confirmed that Xi Jinping will host Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on November 19, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, for the first-ever in-person three-way meeting of the three leaders. Ukraine is not invited, and the White House says the talks will focus on nuclear weapons rather than the war in Ukraine.
articles.body: China's foreign ministry confirmed on Monday that Xi Jinping will host Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on November 19, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, for the first-ever in-person three-way meeting of the leaders of China, the United States and Russia. The confirmation follows days of speculation and the White House announcement last week that the meeting would take place, with the leaders expected to discuss nuclear arms control rather than the war in Ukraine. The Financial Times reported on Monday that the meeting will proceed without a pre-agreed agenda, and that Trump plans to raise nuclear arms control but does not expect to reach an agreement, aiming only to start a discussion between the world's three largest nuclear powers. The Wall Street Journal has reported that it was Putin who proposed the trilateral meeting, hoping to use the summit to agree an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favourable to Moscow. Trump also said on Monday that he intends a separate bilateral meeting with Putin in Shenzhen, and the Kremlin said the two sides are working on the time and format. Ukraine is not invited to the Shenzhen talks, which Kyiv and its European partners will watch closely for any sign of a deal struck over their heads. Media have already dubbed the encounter a 'New Yalta', after the 1945 conference where the Allies divided the post-war world.

articles.title: Crimean Bridge partially reopens after 12 hours closed; Russia claims record 2,049 drones downed
articles.description: Vehicle traffic on the Crimean Bridge was partially restored on Monday evening after being closed for about 12 hours following Ukraine's overnight drone strike, Russian officials said. Russia's defence ministry claimed its air defences shot down 2,049 Ukrainian drones in 24 hours — which state media called the most massive Ukrainian drone attack since the start of the full-scale war.
articles.body: Vehicle traffic on the Crimean Bridge was partially restored on Monday evening, around 19:00 Moscow time, after being closed for about 12 hours following Ukraine's overnight drone strike, Meduza reported, updating the story covered in the morning digest. Traffic had been stopped from about 02:00 Moscow time after the bridge was hit, with the head of annexed Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, saying restrictions would last until around midday; rail traffic resumed earlier in the day while the road section stayed shut for damage assessment. The Kremlin called the damage 'minor', though Russian officials have not disclosed its full extent, and the transport ministry said it was weighing reopening the road in alternating directions. Russia's defence ministry claimed its air defences shot down 2,049 Ukrainian drones over 24 hours, along with four Flamingo missiles — a figure state news agency RIA Novosti described as the most massive Ukrainian drone attack since the start of the full-scale war. The bridge, Russia's only direct land link to occupied Crimea and a key supply route for its forces, has been attacked several times since 2022. Ukraine's defence forces have not commented on the strike. The scale of the claimed drone wave, if accurate, would mark a sharp escalation in the long-range drone war even as peace diplomacy intensifies.

articles.title: Kremlin told United Russia deputies to prepare for 'victory' at closed seminar, Vedomosti and Meduza report
articles.description: Representatives of the Russian presidential administration told United Russia deputies at a seminar on November 13–14 to prepare for the end of the war in Ukraine and for fighters to return home 'all at once', according to Vedomosti, cited by Meduza. The documents do not explain how deputies should prepare, or give a timeline.
articles.body: Representatives of the Russian presidential administration told deputies from the ruling United Russia party to prepare for 'victory' in the war against Ukraine, according to Vedomosti, cited by Meduza. The message was delivered at a seminar held on November 13–14 at the Senezh management training centre outside Moscow, attended by party leader Dmitry Medvedev, first deputy chief of staff Sergei Kiriyenko and other senior Kremlin officials. A source told both outlets that deputies were told 'everyone must be ready for victory, for when the participants in the special military operation return all at once.' The seminar documents do not explain how deputies should prepare for victory, nor do they give any timeline for a return of troops. The Dossier Center has separately reported, cited by The Moscow Times, that the Kremlin is preparing talking points to present any peace deal to the public as a victory. The episode suggests the Kremlin is already thinking about the domestic politics of ending the war, even as fighting continues and no agreement has been reached.

articles.title: Xi–Trump–Putin meeting will have no pre-agreed agenda, Financial Times reports
articles.description: The three-way meeting of Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on November 19 will take place without a pre-agreed agenda, the Financial Times reports, cited by Meduza. Trump plans to raise nuclear arms control but does not expect to reach an agreement — he wants only to start a discussion between the three largest nuclear powers.
articles.body: The three-way meeting of Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen will take place without a pre-agreed agenda, the Financial Times reports, cited by Meduza. According to a US official quoted by the paper, Trump plans to raise nuclear arms control at the talks scheduled for November 19, but 'does not expect to reach an agreement' — he wants only to start a discussion between the world's three largest nuclear powers. The Wall Street Journal earlier reported, citing sources, that disagreements had emerged between the US and China over the format and agenda of the meeting. It was Putin who proposed the trilateral encounter, according to the Journal, hoping to use the summit to agree an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favourable to Moscow. The White House has said Trump will discuss nuclear weapons with Putin and Xi, but not the war in Ukraine — though Trump also said on Monday he wants to discuss the Ukraine settlement with the two leaders in Shenzhen. The absence of an agreed agenda underlines how improvised the historic meeting is, and how uncertain its outcome remains.

articles.title: Could Trump, Putin and Xi 'divide the world' like the Allies at Yalta in 1945? Meduza asks a China expert
articles.description: With the first-ever three-way meeting of Xi, Trump and Putin set for November 19 in Shenzhen, media have already dubbed it a 'New Yalta', after the 1945 conference where the Allies divided the post-war world. In Meduza's 'What Happened' podcast, China expert Alexey Chigadaev assesses whether the three leaders could really carve up the world between them.
articles.body: The first-ever in-person three-way meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, set for November 19 in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit, has already been dubbed a 'New Yalta' in the media — a reference to the 1945 Yalta Conference where the Allied leaders divided the post-war world. In Meduza's 'What Happened' podcast, host Vladislav Gorin asks China expert Alexey Chigadaev of the NEST Centre whether the three leaders could really divide the world between them, and what each of them wants from the encounter. The question matters because the meeting has no pre-agreed agenda, and because Putin is reported to hope the summit will produce an end to the war in Ukraine on Moscow's terms, while Trump wants to open a discussion on nuclear arms control. The Yalta analogy captures both the historic scale of the meeting and the anxiety it provokes — in Kyiv and in European capitals — that a deal could be struck over Ukraine's head. Chigadaev's assessment, published on Monday, is the latest in a series of Meduza explainers trying to make sense of a summit that was unthinkable only weeks ago.

articles.title: Komyshuvakha death toll rises to 72 as search work ends
articles.description: Search operations have finished in Komyshuvakha, and the death toll from Russia's November 15 strike on a humanitarian aid distribution point has risen to 72, up from the 57 reported in the morning. The attack hit a site where civilians were collecting aid, making it one of the deadliest single strikes on civilians in recent weeks.
articles.body: Search and rescue work has been completed in Komyshuvakha, and the death toll from the Russian strike on a humanitarian aid distribution point there has risen to 72 people, Ukrainian authorities said on Monday evening. The morning digest reported at least 57 killed in the November 15 attack, which hit a site in Zaporizhzhia region where civilians were queuing to collect humanitarian aid. The revised figure makes it one of the deadliest single Russian strikes on civilians in recent weeks. The strike came during a weekend of heavy Russian attacks across Ukraine, and it was condemned internationally as a breach of international humanitarian law. No further survivors were found as rescuers finished clearing the rubble. The rising toll underlines how the war's civilian cost keeps climbing even as diplomats push for a ceasefire, and it is likely to feature in Ukraine's arguments for more air-defence support from its partners.

articles.title: Zelenskyy warns Russia is preparing a new missile strike
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on Monday evening that Russia is preparing a new missile strike against Ukraine, as Russian attacks on energy infrastructure left large parts of Dnipro without power. He also described a 'difficult' conversation between Ukrainian, American and European negotiating teams as peace diplomacy intensifies.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on Monday evening that Russia is preparing a new missile strike against Ukraine, according to Ukrainska Pravda's latest-news feed. The warning came as Russia continued its campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with evening strikes knocking out power across much of Dnipro in what officials called the sixth blackout in two weeks. Zelenskyy also said he had spoken about a 'difficult' conversation held between the Ukrainian, American and European negotiating teams, as the diplomacy around ending the war enters its most active phase in months. The warning of a fresh missile attack follows the overnight drone barrage and the strike on the Crimean Bridge, and it suggests Kyiv expects Moscow to keep up military pressure while talks continue. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly said Russia times its strikes on the power grid to maximise hardship as winter approaches, and air-defence supplies remain Kyiv's most urgent request to its partners. The president's comments came hours after the EU approved its largest-ever single payment to Ukraine and transferred a further €1.71 billion for weapons purchases.

articles.title: Sixth blackout in two weeks: Russian strikes leave almost half of Dnipro without power
articles.description: Russian evening strikes on energy facilities left almost half of Dnipro without electricity on Monday — the sixth blackout in two weeks — with power also out across parts of three surrounding districts. Ukrenergo named Dnipro, Kharkiv, Poltava and Zaporizhzhia as the hardest-hit cities, and regional officials reported more than 60 attacks in Dnipropetrovsk region, with two killed and 19 wounded.
articles.body: Russian strikes on energy infrastructure left almost half of Dnipro without power on Monday evening, Ukrainska Pravda reports, in what officials called the sixth blackout in the city in two weeks. Energy company DTEK said the whole city was blacked out after the evening attack on energy facilities, along with parts of the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi and Kamian districts. Grid operator Ukrenergo named four cities as the hardest hit on Monday evening: Dnipro, Kharkiv, Poltava and Zaporizhzhia. The head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional administration, Oleksandr Hanzha, reported more than 60 drone and artillery attacks across the region during the day, with two people killed in Dnipro and 19 wounded, including a 16-year-old boy. The strikes are part of Russia's sustained campaign against Ukraine's power grid as winter approaches, aimed at leaving cities cold and dark. Ukrainian officials say the attacks are designed to break civilian morale, while Kyiv continues to plead with its partners for more air-defence systems and for help repairing the grid. The blackout came on the same day the EU transferred €1.71 billion to Ukraine specifically for drones, missiles and air-defence systems.

articles.title: Putin's office says Europe's role in peace talks 'was not agreed with Russia'
articles.description: The Kremlin said on Monday that Europe's participation in the peace negotiations on Ukraine 'was not agreed with Russia', pushing back against the EU's push for a seat at the table. The comment came as EU foreign ministers confirmed a ceasefire-first negotiating line and rejected Moscow's demands on European security.
articles.body: The Kremlin said on Monday that Europe's participation in the peace negotiations on Ukraine 'was not agreed with Russia', according to Ukrainska Pravda. The statement pushes back against the European Union's efforts to secure a seat at the negotiating table, after EU leaders last week named a delegation to take part in the talks, including representatives of the European Commission, the European Council and the E5 countries — Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland. At a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday, the bloc confirmed its negotiating line: first secure a ceasefire in Ukraine, and only then discuss Moscow's demands and a broader European security settlement. The ministers also rejected Russia's demands on the European security architecture, including Moscow's reported call for NATO forces to return to their 1997 deployments. The Kremlin's objection to Europe's role underlines the central tension in the diplomacy: Moscow would prefer to negotiate directly with Washington, while Kyiv and Brussels insist that no deal on Ukraine or European security can be made without them. The dispute is likely to sharpen as the Shenzhen summit approaches.

articles.title: Kushner: any final peace deal must be agreed by both Russia and Ukraine; multilateral meeting being prepared
articles.description: Jared Kushner, one of President Trump's envoys, said on Monday that any final peace agreement must be agreed by both Russia and Ukraine, and that preparations are under way for a multilateral meeting on the war. The comments came as the US, Ukrainian and European negotiating teams held what Zelenskyy called a 'difficult' conversation.
articles.body: Jared Kushner, one of President Trump's envoys on Ukraine, said on Monday that any final peace agreement must be agreed by both Russia and Ukraine, and that preparations are under way for a multilateral meeting on the war, Ukrainska Pravda reports. Kushner's comments are a notable statement of principle from inside Trump's circle at a moment when Kyiv and its European partners worry that a deal could be struck over their heads — particularly at Thursday's three-way meeting of Trump, Putin and Xi in Shenzhen, to which Ukraine is not invited. The envoy's remarks came on the same day President Zelenskyy described a 'difficult' conversation between the Ukrainian, American and European negotiating teams, suggesting the diplomacy is entering a tense phase. Kushner has been one of the key American intermediaries in the talks, and his insistence on both sides agreeing to any final deal will reassure Kyiv, though it remains to be seen how it squares with the parallel tracks inside Ukraine's own delegation on the Donbas question. A multilateral meeting, if it happens, would be the first to bring all the parties together since the diplomacy accelerated this autumn.

articles.title: US allocates $1.6 billion to speed up production of engines for Patriot missiles
articles.description: The United States has allocated $1.6 billion to accelerate production of engines for Patriot air-defence missiles, Ukrainska Pravda reports, citing its defence outlet. The funding comes as Ukraine pleads for more air-defence systems to protect its cities and power grid from Russian strikes.
articles.body: The United States has allocated $1.6 billion to accelerate production of engines for Patriot air-defence missiles, Ukrainska Pravda reports, citing its defence publication. The funding is aimed at expanding output of the interceptors that have become the backbone of Ukraine's air defences against Russian ballistic missiles, and it comes as Kyiv pleads for more air-defence systems to protect its cities and power grid. Patriot batteries have been critical in intercepting the Russian missiles that drones alone cannot stop, but supplies of interceptors have been a persistent constraint, with production struggling to keep pace with demand. The allocation also reflects Washington's broader push to rebuild its missile stockpiles after years of drawdowns. For Ukraine, the news is welcome but the timelines matter: new production capacity takes months to come online, while Russian strikes on the energy grid are happening now. The funding announcement came on the same day the EU transferred €1.71 billion to Kyiv for drones, missiles and air defence, making Monday one of the biggest single days of Western military-industrial support for Ukraine in months.

articles.title: EU weighs entry bans for Russians who fought in Ukraine — and a ban on Russian athletes under the national flag
articles.description: The EU may receive lists of Russians who fought against Ukraine so they can be barred from entering the bloc, foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, and Brussels is also considering banning Russian athletes from competing under the national flag in a new sanctions package. The measures come as the EU sanctioned 12 more people and 101 organisations over financing Russia's war.
articles.body: The European Union may receive lists of Russians who fought against Ukraine so they can be barred from entering the bloc, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday, and Brussels is also considering banning Russian athletes from competing under the national flag in a new sanctions package. The measures were reported by Ukrainska Pravda as the EU stepped up pressure on Moscow on several fronts at once. Earlier on Monday, the EU Council imposed sanctions on 12 more individuals and 101 organisations for their role in financing Russia's war against Ukraine, expanding restrictions on Russian energy, banking, the shadow fleet, e-commerce and sanctions-evasion networks. The new package also targeted the founder of the Wildberries marketplace, Tatyana Kim, and 49 banks. An entry ban for Russians who fought in Ukraine would be a significant expansion of the EU's sanctions regime, turning the battlefield into a basis for exclusion from Europe. The proposed sports ban would extend the isolation of Russian athletes that began after the full-scale invasion. Both measures still need agreement among member states, but they signal that the EU is not easing pressure on Moscow even as peace talks intensify.

articles.title: Prince Harry meets Ukrainian soldier who was evacuated from the front by drone
articles.description: Prince Harry met a Ukrainian soldier who was evacuated from his position by drone, Ukrainska Pravda reports in a video story. 'I saw you on the news!' the prince told the soldier during the meeting.
articles.body: Prince Harry met a Ukrainian soldier who was evacuated from his position at the front by drone, Ukrainska Pravda reports in a video story published on Monday evening. 'I saw you on the news!' the prince told the soldier during the meeting, which was filmed and shared by the outlet. The encounter is the latest in a series of public appearances by the Duke of Sussex in support of Ukrainian veterans and wounded soldiers, a cause he has championed since the start of the full-scale invasion. Drone evacuations of wounded soldiers have become a striking feature of this war, with unmanned aircraft now used to pull injured troops from positions too dangerous for conventional medevac. The soldier's story had already made the news before the meeting, which is how Harry knew him. The video was one of the most prominent human-interest stories on the Pravda homepage on Monday evening, offering a rare lighter moment on a day dominated by strikes, blackouts and diplomacy.

articles.title: Olha Kharlan announces her return to fencing after 'a big pause'
articles.description: Ukrainian fencing star Olha Kharlan has announced her return to the sport after what she called 'a big pause'. The Olympic champion, one of Ukraine's most decorated athletes, had stepped back from competition.
articles.body: Ukrainian fencing star Olha Kharlan has announced her return to the sport after what she called 'a big pause', Ukrainska Pravda reports. Kharlan, an Olympic champion and one of Ukraine's most decorated athletes, had stepped back from competition, and her announcement ends speculation about her future in the sport. She is one of the most recognisable faces of Ukrainian sport internationally, and her return will be welcomed by fans at home, where she has become a symbol of resilience during the war. Kharlan made global headlines in 2023 when she was disqualified at the World Championships for refusing to shake hands with a Russian opponent, a decision that was later overturned amid an international outcry. Her comeback adds to a strong day for Ukrainian sport, with freediver Kateryna Zharkova also setting a world record at a competition in Dominica on Monday. No date has been given for Kharlan's first competition back, but her announcement suggests she is targeting a return to the piste in the near future.

articles.title: Microsoft is building Xbox Project Helix as a console that can also run PC games
articles.description: Microsoft is developing its next Xbox, codenamed Project Helix, primarily as a console that will also be able to run PC games, lead Xbox engineer Jason Ronald has revealed in a digital magazine marking 25 years of the Xbox brand.
articles.body: Microsoft is developing its next Xbox, codenamed Project Helix, primarily as a console that will also be able to run PC games, lead Xbox engineer Jason Ronald has revealed. Ronald described the plan in a digital magazine released to mark the 25th anniversary of the Xbox brand, which fell on November 15. The hybrid approach would blur the line between console and PC gaming, letting players run their PC libraries on a living-room box — a long-rumoured direction for Microsoft, which owns both the Xbox platform and Windows. The reveal comes as Microsoft celebrates a quarter-century of Xbox with throwback touches, including three historic start-up animations for Series X|S and One and eight classic games joining the base tier of Game Pass. No release date or price has been given for Project Helix, and Microsoft has not said which PC games or storefronts it would support. But the confirmation from a senior engineer is the clearest signal yet that the next Xbox will be a very different kind of machine from its predecessors.

articles.title: EA shakes up Battlefield leadership after the death of Vince Zampella
articles.description: Electronic Arts has reshuffled the leadership of the Battlefield franchise, with Byron Beede no longer its general manager. The changes follow the death of Vince Zampella, the 'father' of Call of Duty, who had been a central figure in Battlefield's revival.
articles.body: Electronic Arts has carried out a reshuffle in the leadership of the Battlefield franchise, GameMAG reports, with Byron Beede no longer serving as the franchise's general manager. The changes appear to follow the death of Vince Zampella, the co-creator of Call of Duty who had become a central figure in Battlefield's revival at EA. Zampella, who founded Respawn Entertainment and led the team behind the Battlefield series' recent direction, died recently, leaving a gap at the top of one of EA's most important franchises. The reshuffle is the first sign of how EA plans to reorganise Battlefield without him, and it comes at a sensitive moment for the series, which has been rebuilding its reputation after a difficult launch for its last entry. EA has not announced a replacement for Beede or a new structure for the franchise's leadership. Fans will be watching closely for whether the changes affect the next Battlefield game, which is expected to be a major test of the series' future.

articles.title: Shooting at inXile Entertainment office in California; no developers hurt, suspect arrested
articles.description: A shooting took place in Tustin, California, with several bullets hitting the office building of inXile Entertainment, the studio behind Wasteland and the upcoming Clockwork Revolution. Xbox said the developers were not hurt, and police have arrested a suspect.
articles.body: A shooting took place in Tustin, California, on Monday, with several bullets hitting the office building of inXile Entertainment, the studio behind Wasteland and the upcoming Clockwork Revolution, GameMAG reports. Local news media reported that the office building was struck by gunfire, and Xbox later confirmed that the developers were not hurt. Police have arrested a suspect, though no motive has been disclosed. inXile, founded by Brian Fargo, is one of Microsoft's Xbox Game Studios and is currently working on Clockwork Revolution, a first-person RPG that is one of the most anticipated titles in Xbox's pipeline. The incident is a reminder of the gun violence that regularly touches American workplaces, including in the games industry. Xbox's swift confirmation that staff were safe will have reassured fans, but the studio has not said whether the shooting will affect its work. The investigation is ongoing.

articles.title: Earning the GTA VI platinum trophy could take around 200 hours
articles.description: Getting the platinum trophy in Grand Theft Auto VI could take around 200 hours, journalist Tom Henderson of Insider Gaming has reported. That is roughly as long as earning every achievement in Red Dead Redemption 2.
articles.body: Earning the platinum trophy in Grand Theft Auto VI could take around 200 hours, journalist Tom Henderson of Insider Gaming has reported, citing his sources. That is roughly as long as it takes to earn every achievement in Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar's last epic, and it suggests GTA VI will be a vast game with an enormous amount of content to complete. The figure will not surprise fans of Rockstar's open worlds, which are famous for their density, but it sets expectations for just how much there is to do in the game's version of Leonida. The report comes three days before the game's launch on Thursday, November 19, when players will finally be able to judge the scale for themselves. It also follows news that the game's soundtrack album features new music from Lana Del Rey, Dua Lipa and Zara Larsson, and that the game includes an in-game cartoon series, 'Macca & Friends'. For completionists, the 200-hour figure is both a warning and a promise: GTA VI is not a game to be rushed.

articles.title: id Software is already working on its next game, Xbox says
articles.description: id Software has already started work on its next game, Xbox boss Asha Sharma has said during the celebrations for the 25th anniversary of the Xbox brand. The studio released the DOOM: The Dark Ages expansion Revelations this year, with its new Slaughter Mode arriving today.
articles.body: id Software has already started work on its next game, Xbox boss Asha Sharma has said during the celebrations marking 25 years of the Xbox brand. 'The team is already working on its next game,' Sharma said, according to GameMAG, without giving any details about what it is. The announcement comes as the studio releases Slaughter Mode, a free endless-wave survival trial, for DOOM: The Dark Ages today, November 16, for all owners of the Revelations expansion. Rumours circulated over the summer that id was already working on a new DOOM, and Sharma's comment confirms the studio is not resting after finishing the expansion. id Software, founded in 1991, created DOOM and Quake and remains one of the most respected studios in first-person shooters. Its next project will be closely watched, whether it turns out to be another DOOM, a revival of Quake, or something entirely new. No release window has been given.

articles.title: Resident Evil Requiem named Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards
articles.description: Capcom's horror game Resident Evil Requiem has been named Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards. Angela Sant-Albano, who plays Grace Ashcroft, won Best Lead Role at the ceremony.
articles.body: Capcom's horror game Resident Evil Requiem has been named Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards, GameMAG reports, in one of the first major awards verdicts of the season. Angela Sant-Albano, who plays the game's protagonist Grace Ashcroft, also won Best Lead Role at the ceremony, capping a strong night for the survival horror sequel. The win confirms Requiem's status as one of the standout releases of the year, and it sets it up as a frontrunner for further awards — with the nominees for The Game Awards 2026 due to be announced tomorrow, November 17. Resident Evil has been one of the most consistent franchises in gaming over the past decade, with Capcom's recent entries winning both critical praise and huge sales. Requiem's Golden Joystick victory suggests the series is still at the top of its game. The ceremony's other winners have not been detailed in the reports so far, but the top prize going to a horror game underlines how broad the year's best releases have been.

articles.title: PIONER shuts down as funding runs out; servers stopped
articles.description: The developers of PIONER have announced the game's closure: development and updates have officially stopped and the game servers have been shut down, because there is no funding to keep the project going.
articles.body: The developers of PIONER have announced that the game is shutting down, GameMAG reports. Development and updates have officially ceased and the game servers have been stopped, with the studio citing a lack of funding as the reason. The team said that keeping the project alive would have required ongoing spending on infrastructure, which it can no longer afford. PIONER was an ambitious multiplayer shooter that had been in development for years, and its closure is a reminder of how tough the market has become for live-service games that fail to find a large enough audience. The announcement will disappoint the players who stuck with it, but the studio's frank explanation — no money, no servers — is unusually direct. The closure comes in a week dominated by the impending launch of GTA VI, which is expected to suck up attention and spending across the industry. PIONER's fate is the other side of that story: for every blockbuster, there are games that simply run out of road.

articles.title: Major US banks hit by online banking outages; Chase says it is a technical issue, not a cyberattack
articles.description: Customers of several major US banks — Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Truist — reported widespread problems accessing online banking on Monday, with thousands of complaints logged on Downdetector. Chase, the worst hit with nearly 5,000 reports, confirmed a technical issue and said customers still have access to their accounts and funds; it is not a cyberattack.
articles.body: Customers of several of America's largest banks reported widespread problems accessing their accounts on Monday, November 16, as technical disruptions hit online banking websites, mobile apps and some transactions across the United States. JPMorgan Chase was the worst affected, with nearly 5,000 user reports on the outage-tracking site Downdetector by early afternoon, followed by Bank of America with roughly 2,000 and Wells Fargo with more than 1,000, plus reports at U.S. Bank, Truist and the payment service Zelle. Chase confirmed the disruption stems from an internal technical bug rather than a cybersecurity incident, saying in a statement that 'some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds.' Wells Fargo's website said online banking was temporarily unavailable, while U.S. Bank said its own systems were not directly hit but warned that Zelle payments involving other banks could be delayed. The Federal Reserve's service-status page still showed normal operations for Fedwire, FedACH and FedNow, and no statement came from the FDIC, CISA or the Treasury. The outages followed a major Microsoft service disruption on Friday and the nationwide FAA ground stop, though no connection between the incidents has been confirmed. As of Monday afternoon the precise cause had not been established and Chase had not given a time for full restoration.

articles.title: Trump administration tightens AI chip export curbs ahead of China trip
articles.description: The Commerce Department has tightened export restrictions designed to keep sensitive, AI-powering computer chips out of China's hands, just as President Trump departs for Asia and a historic three-way meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. The move comes amid scrutiny of how strictly the chip controls have been enforced, and as Trump said he 'would not mind' if Nvidia's Jensen Huang were reinstated.
articles.body: The Trump administration has tightened restrictions on the flow of AI chips ahead of the president's trip to China, CNN reports, with the Commerce Department moving to close gaps in export controls designed to prevent Beijing from accessing the sensitive computer chips that power artificial intelligence. The decision lands as Trump departs Monday for the Philippines, the ASEAN summit in Manila and APEC in Shenzhen, where he is due to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in an unprecedented three-way session on Thursday. Enforcement of the chip controls has come under scrutiny, with CNN reporting on how Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick cultivated a close relationship with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang while controls slipped, and on the wider stakes of the Nvidia story beyond the personalities involved. Trump added a twist on Monday by saying he 'would not mind' if Huang were reinstated at Nvidia, after the Financial Times reported that the former Nvidia president could return to the top job. The tightened curbs signal that, even as Trump seeks a headline meeting with Xi, his administration is not easing the technology rivalry that has defined US-China relations. The controls remain one of Washington's main levers over Beijing's AI ambitions, and any softening would have been read in China as a concession.

articles.title: What we know about the Mississippi river collision that capsized a cruise ship
articles.description: A tanker lost steering when its rudder froze and struck a docked riverboat in New Orleans on Friday, capsizing it within 22 minutes. All 190 people aboard survived, 32 were taken to hospital, and four remained there on Monday. Federal investigators are now interviewing the crew and studying the ships' recordings.
articles.body: A tanker suddenly lost control of its steering when its rudder froze, pushing the ship into a docked riverboat in New Orleans on Friday and capsizing it within 22 minutes, federal investigators say. The riverboat, an American Cruise Lines vessel docked at the Thalia Street Wharf, had 140 passengers and 50 crew aboard; all survived, with 32 taken to hospital and four still there on Monday morning, one in serious condition and three stable. The tanker had 19 crew members and one local pilot aboard and was headed to an oil facility upriver. The National Transportation Safety Board said its investigation will include preserving evidence from both ships, listening to recordings and interviewing passengers and crew, with crew interviews beginning Monday; the probe is not criminal in nature. The Port of New Orleans filed a lawsuit against the tanker's owners, Thome Ship Management of Singapore and the vessel's listed owner Nave Shipping, hours after the crash, saying the tanker caused more than $1 million in damage to a New Orleans terminal through 'negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness'. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry called it a 'miracle on the Mississippi' that everyone made it to safety. The focus of the investigation is the steering failure that left the rudder stuck fully to starboard, and whether personnel, the ships or the environment at the time played a role.

articles.title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest Pearl Harbor survivor, dies at 106
articles.description: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, has died at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106. Johnson was below deck on the USS St. Louis when the Japanese attack happened on December 7, 1941, and later said he neither heard nor saw it.
articles.body: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, has died at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts, his daughter Diane Johnson said. He was 106. Johnson was one of an estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on December 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In an interview with the Associated Press in May 2026, he said he didn't hear or see the attack. The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the death in December 2025 of Ira 'Ike' Schab, who was 105. Johnson's death leaves that small group smaller still, and it comes as the 85th anniversary of the attack approaches next month. The Pearl Harbor survivors have long been honoured at annual commemorations in Hawaii, and their passing marks the gradual fading of living memory of the day that brought the United States into the Second World War.

articles.title: Pope Leo's return to Latin America draws 12 million people after lung cancer surgery
articles.description: Pope Leo XIV's 12-day visit to South America drew more than 12 million people to papal events and Masses, just weeks after he underwent lung cancer surgery.
